articles.title: Robbie Williams' surprise singalong after Peru gig cancelled
articles.summary: Robbie Williams gave an impromptu performance outside a hotel in Lima after his stadium concert was cancelled.
articles.body:
Robbie Williams gave an impromptu performance outside a hotel in Peru's capital Lima, after his concert at a stadium in the city was cancelled.

Authorities announced that the Arena 1 Park gig could not go ahead, citing failures by the venue to comply with safety regulations.

Robbie told fans outside his hotel he was "broken-hearted" and held a brief singalong with the cheering crowds.

articles.title: Powerful Hurricane Polo drenches Mexico's coast as Nolo takes aim at Hawaii
articles.summary: Residents along Mexico’s west coast stacked sandbags to fortify beachfront shops and evacuated their homes, while Hawaii’s Big Island and Maui braced for pot...
articles.body:
MEXICO CITY (AP) — Residents along Mexico's west coast stacked sandbags to fortify beachfront shops and evacuated their homes, while Hawaii's Big Island and Maui braced for potentially catastrophic flooding, as separate hurricanes swirled in the Pacific on Thursday.

Nolo became a hurricane in the Pacific Ocean on Thursday night and was expected to strengthen while turning toward the Big Island, the National Hurricane Center said. Forecasters warned that the Big Island could see rainfall totals of 15 to 30 inches (38 to 76 centimeters), with higher amounts possible through Saturday. The island of Maui also could be hit with life-threatening floods, the hurricane center said.

Meanwhile, heavy rains from powerful Hurricane Polo could cause torrential flooding and landslides in Mexico, according to the U.S. hurricane center. In the port city of Lázaro Cárdenas, seawater already swept through homes Thursday and left wooden planks and furniture strewn on the streets.

Polo has fluctuated between Category 4 and 5, both major-hurricane strength. It was expected to regain Category 5 status on Friday, then gradually weaken Friday night and Saturday, the hurricane center said.

After skirting Mexico's coast, Polo was expected to move farther out to sea Thursday night and Friday before hooking back toward land to the north on Saturday.

The series of powerful storms comes as the weather phenomenon El Niño prompts major environmental shifts across the world, fueling drought in some areas and flooding in others. El Niño traditionally dampens the Atlantic hurricane season , while it tends to rev up tropical cyclone activity in the Pacific with moist air and little wind shear.

Hawaii has been battered this year by major flooding in the spring, an earthquake and two other hurricanes since mid-August.

"In my 20 years of experience here, I've never seen three hurricane watches for the islands in the same year," said John Bravender of the National Weather Service in Honolulu.

Polo could trigger flooding and mudslides in Mexico

Mexican authorities were opening shelters and clearing people from beaches, while coastal residents tried to protect businesses from getting swept away. People in high-risk areas were being evacuated, though authorities didn't immediately say how many.

Much of the worry from locals comes from hurricanes in past years that devastated cities along the Pacific coast. Hurricane Otis in 2023 unexpectedly plunged Acapulco into turmoil for weeks.

"So many people said it wouldn't happen and then it did. After that, you're left on edge," said Gonzalo Ramírez, a bartender in the city.

Polo posed the biggest threat to Guerrero and Michoacán, neighboring states in southwest Mexico that share a long coastline scattered with small ports, tourist towns and fishing villages. Much of the area is marked by poverty , and residents routinely complain they are left to fend for themselves during natural disasters.

Mexican authorities have deployed 15,000 security personnel across the coast and suspended schools.

In Lázaro Cárdenas, a port city in Michoacán that was hit with high surf, locals and government officials were clearing out piles of wooden planks from a number of destroyed ramadas and shoveling thick mud coating much of the town.

Alicia Contreras said the walls and roof of her restaurant had been severely damaged by 15-foot (4.5-meter) waves. As officers and family helped pick through the damaged house, Contreras worried how she would economically recover.

"This is huge because we have no other source of income. Now we're just surviving," Contreras said.

Nolo could flood parts of Hawaii still recovering from other storms

While the Big Island is expected to bear the brunt of Nolo, its full path remains uncertain, according to Bravender, the weather service's warning coordination meteorologist in Hawaii.

Most concerning, he said Thursday, is that the heaviest rain is likely to fall over the same southeastern region of the Big Island hit in August by Hurricane Lala and where grounds are still wet from additional precipitation.

"There are several communities that were isolated, flooded, roads that were washed out," he said. "It's that same area that is most under threat," Bravender said.

Hawaii officials told residents to put together emergency kits and the governor issued an emergency proclamation, activating more than 230 Hawaii National Guard members. Schools were closed for the rest of the week.

Hawaiian Electric, the state's primary utility, said crews that had been helping restore power in Kauai after this month's Hurricane Lowell would return to Oahu, Maui and the Big Island in preparation for the coming storm.

A third storm in the Pacific, Hurricane Odalys, was centered far from land, roughly 1,110 miles (1,785 kilometers) west-southwest of the southern tip of Mexico's Baja California peninsula.

In the northern Atlantic Ocean, Tropical Storm Fay re-formed early Thursday, the U.S. hurricane center said. It was nearly 1,000 miles (1,600 kilometers) west-southwest of the Azores.

Tropical Storm Gonzalo formed in the Atlantic Ocean late Thursday, about 190 miles (306 kilometers) southeast of the Cape Verde islands off the coast of West Africa. The U.S. hurricane center said that if it stays on its current track, the storm will pass near or over portions of the islands Friday.

Aoun Angueira reported from San Diego. Associated Press journalists John Seewer in Toledo, Ohio, Hannah Schoenbaum in Salt Lake City and Jeriel Vargas Ambriz in Lázaro Cárdena, Mexico, contributed to this report.
authors: MEGAN JANETSKY and GABRIELA AOUN ANGUEIRA

articles.title: Imagineland 2026: Homenagem a Shaolin marca abertura do evento | G1
articles.standfirst: Homenagem marca inauguração de teatro que leva o nome do humorista. Evento acontece no Centro de Convenções de Campina Grande e terá mais de 160 horas de programação, com artistas de 'High School Musical', 'One Piece', 'The Vampire Diaries' e 'Power Rangers'.
articles.summary: Imagineland 2026 inicia em Campina Grande com tributo a Shaolin e astros de High School Musical e One Piece em mais de 160 horas de programação.
articles.body:
Morte do humorista completa um ano neste sábado — Foto: Reprodução/TV Paraíba

O Imagineland On The Road 2026 começa nesta sexta-feira (25), em Campina Grande , no Agreste da Paraíba, com uma homenagem ao humorista paraibano Shaolin.

A cerimônia de abertura está marcada para as 13h e também inaugura o teatro que leva o nome do humorista, no Centro de Convenções de Campina Grande.

O evento acontece até domingo (27) e terá mais de 160 horas de programação, distribuídas em diferentes espaços, com atrações nacionais e internacionais.

Entre os destaques da programação estão Corbin Bleu , Lucas Grabeel e Monique Coleman , do elenco de "High School Musical", que participam das comemorações dos 20 anos do primeiro filme. Também estão confirmados a atriz Lera Abova , de "One Piece: A Série"; o ator Zach Roerig , de "The Vampire Diaries"; Walter Jones , de "Power Rangers"; e o ator e cantor sul-coreano Lee Jin-hyuk .

Além dos artistas internacionais, o evento terá painéis com dubladores, exibição de filmes, séries e animes, atrações de K-pop e doramas, torneios de games, luta medieval e espaços para quadrinistas e artistas.

Imagineland 2026 começa nesta sexta (25) com atrações internacionais em Campina Grande — Foto: Foto: Montagem/g1

A programação será distribuída em cinco espaços principais: Teatro Shaolin, Red Carpet Claro TV+, Claro Gaming Zone, Artists’ Alley e Arena Medieval. O evento também terá estandes de marcas, praça de alimentação, Arena Dance e Arena Laser Tag.

Os portões serão abertos às 11h e o evento segue até as 21h. O passaporte dá acesso aos espaços do Imagineland, com exceção da área de fotos e autógrafos, que é cobrada à parte.

Nesta sexta-feira (25), primeiro dia de evento, a entrada é gratuita para estudantes de escolas da rede pública de ensino. As vagas são limitadas.

O Imagineland 2026 também terá transporte oficial entre João Pessoa e Campina Grande. O serviço sai do Espaço Cultural José Lins do Rêgo, na capital, a partir das 8h, com retorno previsto para às 21h.

O transporte é vendido separadamente e há opções para um, dois ou os três dias do evento.

Os ingressos para o Imagineland são vendidos pela internet, pelo site oficial do evento.

articles.title: Abertas inscrições para Encontro de Produtores de Vinhos do Nordeste e Feira Sertão de Vinhos  | G1
articles.standfirst: Eventos serão nos dias 21 e 22 de outubro no campus IFSertãoPE Petrolina Zona Rural. Interessados em palestras e degustações devem se inscrever pela internet.
articles.summary: Eventos serão nos dias 21 e 22 de outubro no campus IFSertãoPE Petrolina Zona Rural. Interessados em palestras e degustações devem se inscrever pela internet.
articles.body:
Taça de vinho do Vale do São Francisco — Foto: Rita Barbosa/Arquivo pessoal

Petrolina , no Sertão de Pernambuco, sedia nos dias 21 e 22 de outubro o 1º Encontro de Produtores de Vinhos do Nordeste e a 3ª Feira Sertão de Vinhos. Organizados pelo Instituto Federal do Sertão Pernambucano (IF Sertão-PE), os eventos buscam valorizar a produção local e celebrar o Dia do Enólogo (22).

As inscrições são gratuitas e ficam abertas até 21 de outubro pela internet . A programação é voltada para produtores, profissionais, pesquisadores, estudantes e outros representantes do setor de vinhos.

As atividades começam na manhã do dia 21, com palestras e mesas-redondas no auditório do campus Petrolina Zona Rural. Os debates vão abordar temas como os tipos de uvas ideais para os diferentes solos e climas do Nordeste, tecnologias para a produção de espumantes e oportunidades de negócios no mercado.

No dia 22, das 16h às 20h, o campus recebe a 3ª Feira Sertão de Vinhos. O público poderá conhecer e degustar bebidas produzidas pela Escola do Vinho do IF Sertão-PE e por empresas parceiras da região.

articles.title: VÍDEO: embaixador de Israel na ONU provoca diplomata iraniano | G1
articles.standfirst: Incidente ocorreu após discurso do premiê israelense, Benjamin Netanyahu, na quinta (24). Danny Danon foi até representante da comitiva do Irã e disse a ele que torce por mudança de regime no país rival.
articles.summary: Incidente ocorreu após discurso do premiê israelense, Benjamin Netanyahu, na quinta (24). Danny Danon foi até representante da comitiva do Irã e disse a ele que torce por mudança de regime no país rival.
articles.body:
O embaixador de Israel na ONU , Danny Danon, provocou cara a cara um diplomata iraniano dentro do plenário da Assembleia Geral e publicou a interação nas redes sociais com recados ao Irã .

No vídeo, é possível ver Danon se aproximando do diplomata, que representava a comitiva do Irã no plenário da ONU naquele momento, e oferecendo um modem da Starlink, a internet por satélite de Elon Musk. Ele disse também que Israel "ama o povo iraniano" e que torce por mudança de regime no país rival. Veja acima.

"Achei que seria apropriado te dar [o modem da] Starlink. Se você ouviu o [discurso do] premiê [Netanyahu], seria bem útil para vocês para permitir liberdade ao povo iraniano após o que vocês fizeram com eles. (...) Amamos o povo iranianos e rezamos por mudança de regime no Irã, isso ocorrerá um dia", afirmou Danon durante a interação. Mais tarde, nas redes sociais, ele disse que Teerã "prefere continuar oprimindo seu povo".

O modem da Starlink fez alusão à proibição da internet no Irã imposta pelo regime iraniano durante a sangrenta repressão aos protestos antirregime pelo país no início do ano.

O diplomata iraniano envolvido no incidente é Nassed Asadi, conselheiro da missão permanente do Irã na ONU. Ele não respondeu à abordagem de Danon e ficou com o rosto virado para outro lado durante toda a interação. O Irã não havia se pronunciado de forma oficial sobre o incidente até a última atualização desta reportagem.

Embaixador de Israel na ONU, Danny Danon, provoca diplomata iraniano no plenário da Assembleia Geral em 24 de setembro de 2026. — Foto: Divulgação/Danny Danon no X

É possível ver que o vídeo foi gravado após o discurso do premiê israelense, Benjamin Netanyahu , na Assembleia Geral da ONU porque havia uma outra autoridade com a palavra no púlpito no momento da abordagem de Danon.

Em seu discurso na quinta-feira, Netanyahu disse que salvou o mundo com a guerra contra o Irã —que ainda está em andamento e sem perspectiva de ser finalizada— e rebateu acusações de genocídio feitas contra Israel pela comunidade internacional por conta da guerra em Gaza. A delegação do Brasil e de diversos outros países deixaram o plenário da ONU logo antes da fala do premiê israelense.

Após o discurso de Netanyahu, Asadi disse à presidência da Assembleia Geral que o discurso de Netanyahu foi uma "desgraça extrema" para a ONU e um insulto aos valores da organização multilateral, segundo a agência estatal iraniana Irna.

articles.title: Partido de Putin fica com 349 das 450 cadeiras do Parlamento russo | G1
articles.standfirst: A Rússia anunciou, nesta sexta (25), os resultados finais das eleições legislativas da semana passada, confirmando uma vitória esmagadora para o partido do presidente e a eleição de 46 soldados ou veteranos da guerra na Ucrânia como deputados.
articles.summary: A Comissão Eleitoral Central da Rússia confirmou a vitória recorde do partido de Putin e a entrada de 46 veteranos da guerra na Ucrânia para o Parlamento nesta sexta (25).
articles.body:
A Rússia anunciou, nesta sexta-feira (25), os resultados finais das eleições legislativas da semana passada, confirmando uma vitória esmagadora para o partido do presidente Vladimir Putin e a eleição de 46 soldados ou veteranos da guerra na Ucrânia como deputados.

Durante uma coletiva de imprensa, a Comissão Eleitoral Central indicou que 349 das 450 cadeiras da câmara baixa do Parlamento, a Duma, pertencem ao partido Rússia Unida, de Putin.

Este é um número recorde de cadeiras para o partido desde que Putin chegou ao poder , na véspera de Ano Novo de 1999. Seu melhor resultado anterior havia sido nas eleições de 2016, com 343 cadeiras.

Ucraniano vota em eleições parlamentares da Rússia ao lado de soldado russo armado com fuzil na Donetsk ocupada, na Ucrânia, em 18 de setembro de 2026. — Foto: REUTERS/Alexander Ermochenko

Apenas partidos que apoiam, em diferentes graus, Putin e a continuação do conflito na Ucrânia foram autorizados a participar. O único partido abertamente contrário à guerra, Yabloko, foi excluído.

O jornal investigativo no exílio Novaya Gazeta Europa, banido na Rússia por ser considerado uma "organização indesejável", afirmou ter entrevistado observadores, candidatos e membros de partidos que relataram fraudes generalizadas.

Segundo essa fonte, os casos relatados incluíam pressão sobre eleitores, problemas com as cédulas, irregularidades durante a apuração dos votos e restrições ao acesso de observadores ao processo.

Segundo os resultados oficiais, o Partido Comunista da Federação Russa (KPRF) conquistou 37 cadeiras, o partido nacionalista LDPR, 23, o partido Novo Povo, 19, o partido Rússia Justa, 17 e o partido Rodina ("Pátria"), 1 cadeira.

Quatro cadeiras adicionais serão ocupadas por deputados independentes.

Estas eleições também marcam a entrada no Parlamento de indivíduos que lutaram no front ucraniano.

Segundo a Comissão Eleitoral, 46 dos deputados eleitos, mais de 10% do total, são "participantes ou ex-combatentes" da ofensiva em larga escala contra a Ucrânia .

Segundo esta fonte, 41 deles são membros do partido governista Rússia Unida.

articles.title: De inimigo a parceiro: a guinada de Delcy Rodríguez sobre Trump e EUA | G1
articles.standfirst: Presidente interina da Venezuela rompe com a retórica chavista, ignora Nicolás Maduro e deixa transparecer subserviência ao presidente americano na ONU.
articles.summary: Presidente interina da Venezuela rompe com a retórica chavista, ignora Nicolás Maduro e deixa transparecer subserviência ao presidente americano na ONU.
articles.body:
Sete anos separam dois discursos de Delcy Rodríguez na ONU e realçam discrepâncias na retórica belicosa que marcava as relações com os Estados Unidos .

Em 2019, a então vice-presidente da Venezuela exaltou Nicolás Maduro , a quem representava, e execrou Donald Trump , por reconhecer Juan Guaidó como presidente legítimo do país.

"Venho em nome da única Venezuela, a Venezuela digna e corajosa, que não se curva a nenhum poder imperial”, declarou na época.

De volta à Assembleia Geral das Nações Unidas, agora como presidente interina, Rodríguez deixou transparecer a subserviência desmedida ao presidente americano , a quem agradeceu pela disposição de "retomar o caminho das relações diplomáticas e da cooperação com a Venezuela". Sequer mencionou o nome do ex-chefe, capturado em janeiro por forças especiais americanas e transferido, como réu, para uma prisão a 15 quilômetros do palco da ONU .

“A Venezuela deve definitivamente abandonar o caminho que permitiu que o extremismo e a intolerância prevalecessem sobre a convivência democrática e pacífica”, proferiu.

As palavras de Rodríguez nas duas ocasiões ressaltam a dissonância no seu papel como uma das principais representantes do chavismo. A retórica anti-imperialista deu lugar à linguagem da cooperação com Washington.

A lealdade mudou de figura e o antigo inimigo passou a ser apresentado como parceiro. Os gestos do primeiro encontro com o presidente americano refletiram esta guinada: Trump levantou o dedo polegar, Delcy fez o V, de quem a salvou a própria pele, distanciando-se de Maduro e marcando posição a serviço do governo dos EUA.

Trump e Delcy Rodríguez se encontraram na noite de terça-feira (22/9), em Nova York — Foto: X/Delcy Rodríguez

A ruptura da presidente interina com a retórica bolivariana pontuou o discurso de 18 minutos no púlpito da ONU. Ela elogiou o acordo petrolífero firmado com os EUA, que dará ao país o direito de explorar um quinto das reservas de petróleo bruto da Venezuela . Citou expressões pouco usuais ao repertório chavista, como “transformação democrática”, “república pluralista” e “democracia plena”, para descrever os rumos de seu país.

Por fim, Delcy Rodríguez anunciou a realização de eleições, sem especificar prazo , mas dando a impressão de ter sido pressionada a incluir o tópico em seu discurso.

Enquanto a presidente interina da Venezuela estava em Nova York, a líder opositora, María Corina Machado, fazia três tentativas malsucedidas de retornar ao país pelo Panamá . Outrora incensada pelo governo americano, a Prêmio Nobel da Paz vem sendo escanteada por Trump para que não atrapalhe seus planos na transição política e econômica do país .

Em comum, Rodríguez e Machado vêm digerindo doses de humilhação pública administradas por Trump, até agora o maior vencedor da nova ordem de comando do país caribenho . Do púlpito das Nações Unidas ele gabou-se da vitória com a sentença: “Aos vencedores, os despojos.”

A aproximação com Delcy Rodríguez, contudo, preocupa republicanos e desagrada à comunidade latina nos EUA. Pode custar caro ao presidente em novembro.

articles.title: Acidente entre moto e carro deixa ferido na Via Dutra, em Resende | G1
articles.standfirst: Colisão aconteceu na altura do km 300, na pista sentido Rio de Janeiro.
articles.summary: Acidente na Via Dutra em Resende feriu um motociclista no km 300 nesta sexta-feira; o tráfego no sentido Rio de Janeiro já foi normalizado pela concessionária.
articles.body:
Um acidente entre moto e carro deixou uma pessoa ferida na manhã desta sexta-feira (25) na Via Dutra, em Resende (RJ). A colisão aconteceu na altura do km 300, na pista sentido Rio de Janeiro, por volta das 7h53.

Segundo a CCR RioSP, concessionária que administra a rodovia, a vítima, que estava na motocicleta, sofreu ferimentos moderados e recebeu atendimento médico da equipe de resgate da concessionária.

Ainda de acordo com a CCR, durante o atendimento da ocorrência, o tráfego de veículos fluiu pela faixa da direita.

A concessionária também informou que por volta de 8h51, o tráfego de veículos na faixa 1 foi liberada. Não houve registro de lentidão no trecho.

Até a publicação dessa reportagem, a dinâmica do acidente, a identidade dos envolvidos e o estado de saúde da vítima eram desconhecidos.

articles.title: Cursos gratuitos da Bracell capacitam 115 pessoas e ampliam renda na região | G1
articles.standfirst: Projeto Formação Profissional ofereceu 400 horas de capacitação em 10 cursos gratuitos realizados em cinco municípios da região.
articles.summary: Projeto Formação Profissional ofereceu 400 horas de capacitação em 10 cursos gratuitos realizados em cinco municípios da região.
articles.body:
Participantes do curso de Auxiliar de Eletricista durante atividade prática do projeto Formação Profissional, promovido pela Bracell em parceria com o Senai e apoio das prefeituras municipais — Foto: Acervo Bracell

Aprender a operar uma máquina de costura , fazer reparos elétricos ou desenvolver habilidades que podem se transformar em uma nova oportunidade profissional ou fonte de renda. Essa foi a experiência de 115 pessoas de cinco municípios — Agudos (no Distrito de Domélia); Álvaro de Carvalho; Itatinga; Oriente; e Marília (no Distrito de Rosália) — que participaram gratuitamente do projeto Formação Profissional , promovido pela Bracell com execução do Senai e apoio das prefeituras municipais, entre maio e julho de 2026.

Nesta edição, foram oferecidas 400 horas de formação , entre aulas teóricas e práticas , distribuídas em 10 cursos gratuitos , nas áreas de elétrica, mecânica automotiva, alimentação, pintura residencial e costura.

O projeto tem como propósito contribuir para o desenvolvimento das comunidades por meio da educação e da qualificação profissional, ampliando as possibilidades de inserção no mercado de trabalho e de geração de renda.

Além do aprendizado técnico, a iniciativa busca fortalecer a autonomia dos participantes e prepará-los para diferentes possibilidades profissionais.

Conhecimento que ganha aplicação prática

As histórias dos participantes mostram como os conhecimentos adquiridos durante as formações podem ser aplicados em diferentes contextos.

“Eu fiquei muito feliz quando o curso veio para Rosália, pois foi uma oportunidade de aprender. Eu não sabia nada sobre a máquina overloque e, com as aulas práticas, consegui aprender a utilizá-la e fazer os exercícios. Foi uma experiência muito boa e o conhecimento foi enriquecedor”, afirma.

No momento, eu ainda não trabalho nesta área, mas, depois de fazer o curso, já consegui trocar o chuveiro da minha casa, instalar holofotes e arrumar tomadas. Penso nisso também como uma forma de gerar uma renda extra”, conta.

Para os participantes, a formação amplia possibilidades ao transformar conhecimento em aplicação prática, seja no mercado de trabalho, na geração de renda, no empreendedorismo ou no próprio cotidiano.

Para a Bracell , o projeto reforça o compromisso de contribuir para o desenvolvimento das comunidades onde atua, por meio de iniciativas que ampliam o acesso à formação técnica, fortalecem a autonomia e criam novas oportunidades profissionais.

articles.title: NI economy: Economic output rises, but businesses warn of rising costs
articles.summary: Northern Ireland's economic output, which is broadly equivalent to UK GDP, rose by 2.3% in the year to June.
articles.body:
When Greg Bradley started the his gym equipment company 14 years ago, someone told him he would never sell outside the island of Ireland.

"I remember thinking, 'I'm going to prove you wrong'," he said. "Thankfully, we have been able to do that."

BLK BOX is based in Newtownabbey - but it has secured contracts with high-profile customers all over the world, from sports teams like Manchester United to chains like PureGym.

Bradley is just one of many success stories, with official figures showing economic activity in Northern Ireland in the second quarter of this year grew faster than the UK and Republic of Ireland.

BLK BOX works internationally across the EU and markets like the US, Sri Lanka, Maldives, India, Australia and has grown its workforce to 180 staff.

Bradley said Covid had made people realise the importance of their health and "a lot of young people are into going to the gym".

"We have won high profile contracts and expanding internationally across France, Spain, Germany and other countries," he told BBC News NI.

He added that the Windsor Framework had also been advantageous compared to English competitors.

"We've been able to win a contract with a large French gym chain, Stade Français rugby team, so it's actually worked out good for us and we are really doubling down on that.

"There's still a bit of an education process with it, not everyone knows that we can ship frictionlessly across Europe, they are a bit scared of tariffs but once you explain it, everyone is really interested."

Figures from the Northern Ireland Statistics and Research Agency (NISRA) show Northern Ireland's economic output, which is broadly equivalent to UK GDP, rose by 1% in the second quarter to June and by 2.3% over the year.

UK GDP increased by 0.4% over the second quarter and by 1.2% over the year.

Ireland's GDP increased by 10.2% over the second quarter, but its Modified Domestic Demand (MDD), which removes the distorting effects of globalisation, experienced a decline of 0.8% over the quarter.

The growth in Northern Ireland was driven by an increase in the production sector, which includes manufacturing.

Output in the services sector, which is the largest part of the Northern Ireland economy, also increased in the last 12 months.

While these figures suggest the Northern Ireland economy ended the first half of this year in a position of strength, there are real concerns that rising energy and food costs could put businesses under significant pressure in the months ahead.

Pastry chef Daniel Duckett closed his east Belfast patisserie in the last year, but has now re-opened in partnership with Knott's bakery chain in Forestside shopping centre.

Duckett said that Knott's has the buying power for ingredients so "they can control costs a little bit better than we would have been able to".

"They have been able to absorb a lot more of the costs that we would have been paying before," he added.

Duckett said rising petrol prices in particular would affect the cost of goods.

He added: "We have to think, how much do we deliver to the shops? Because that will also affect our petrol prices that fill up vans that travel across Northern Ireland."

He said weather and global warming also affected many products the business brings in, such as tropical fruits, vanilla, cocoa, sugar cane.

"Those are things that are definitely affected by storms and El Niño . I would try to brace myself for that as well."

Duckett added: "For the second half of the year we will have to be vigilant about where those products that have to travel far come from, as petrol prices will have to factor in to that."

articles.title: After rejecting the bus and subway, a New Jersey marketing executive kayaked to Manhattan and walked to work; four years on, his Hudson commute took only 45 minutes
articles.summary: Discover how marketing executive Zach Schwitzky turned his frustrating commute into a daily kayak journey across the Hudson River to Manhattan, cutting travel time to just 45 minutes and blending exercise with work.
articles.body: For most commuters, crossing the Hudson River means taking a train, waiting for a bus or paying for a ferry. For Zach Schwitzky, the journey from Hoboken, New Jersey, to Manhattan became a daily paddle. What began as an unusual response to a frustrating commute became a routine that combined his trip to work with exercise, quiet time and a direct route across the river.According to Gant News, Schwitzky and his friend Erik Barber began kayaking to Manhattan in 2012 after growing tired of their usual commute. Four years later, Schwitzky was still making the crossing, with his journey from home in Hoboken to his workplace taking about 45 minutes in total. He spent roughly 20 minutes kayaking across the Hudson, then walked the rest of the way to his office.From a late-night bus stop to the HudsonThe idea came from frustration rather than from a formal transport experiment. Schwitzky and Barber worked in digital media and dealt with the usual hassles of getting between Hoboken and Manhattan. In 2012, they decided to look for a way of crossing the river on their own terms. CBS News notes that their first attempts were far from the polished routine Schwitzky would later describe. The pair had relatively little kayaking experience and initially paddled the Hudson together. They began making the journey in February 2012, sometimes wearing wetsuits as they dealt with the cold water. By June, they were averaging four days a week on the river.The water crossing was less than a mile, but the commute involved much more than paddling. Usually, they set off from Hoboken and headed to Pier 66 near West 26th Street in Manhattan. At times, they would dock their kayaks at the marina, while at other times, they would carry them by pushing them on the street to reach their workplace. At one point, Schwitzky even moved his 12-foot kayak through Manhattan using a dolly. The unusual sight drew plenty of attention along the way. They also had to make logistical arrangements, especially to keep workplace equipment dry.A 45-minute commute with a very different viewBy 2016, the novelty had worn off for Schwitzky. Commuting by kayak had become part of his daily routine. He would spend twenty minutes paddling, after which he would walk to his office and complete his journey in about 45 minutes. The arrangement had clear benefits. Schwitzky was not bound to the schedules of the buses or trains, and could leave work whenever he wished. The commute also doubled as his exercise routine, especially since he worked long hours as an entrepreneur.The river also offered something public transport could not: a quiet sense of escape. Those who set out early could find themselves paddling through morning fog or watching the sun rise as the Manhattan skyline slowly appeared across the water. But the trip came with its own risks. Paddlers had to keep an eye out for water taxis, barges and the wakes they left behind, which could suddenly make the water rough. For that reason, they had to leave before 7 a.m., before the river became busier with boat traffic.When exercise became part of the journeyAccording to research published in Preventive Medicine, walking and cycling to work were linked to better physical wellbeing among working adults, although the study did not find a significant link with mental wellbeing. The research did not look at kayaking, but it helps explain why turning a commute into a form of exercise could have appealed to Schwitzky.For Schwitzky, the kayak was not just a way to get to work. It gave him a chance to exercise, spend some quiet time on the water and clear his head before the working day began. After four years, what had once seemed like an unusual commute had become part of his everyday routine. While other commuters dealt with traffic and crowded trains, Schwitzky simply picked up his paddle and crossed the river.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: An explosion near the Acropolis in Greece injures at least 2 people and collapses a building
articles.summary: A powerful blast shook the Greek capital’s tourist district of Plaka, near the ancient Acropolis, on Friday morning, causing a building to collapse and injuring at least two people who had to be rescued from an adjacent building, authorities said.
articles.body: A powerful blast shook the Greek capital’s tourist district of Plaka, near the ancient Acropolis, on Friday morning, causing a building to collapse and injuring at least two people who had to be rescued from an adjacent building, authorities said. The fire department said the explosion occurred in an old two-story building in the Plaka district, the historic part of Athens that lies at the foot of the Acropolis hill, Greece’s most visited ancient monument. The building collapsed, while neighboring buildings were also damaged. Firefighters rescued two women from an adjacent building, with police saying both were being transported to a hospital. Local media said a passer-by was also slightly injured by the blast. Police cordoned off the area, while the fire department said rescue crews were checking whether any more people might be trapped. Video footage from the scene showed rubble strewn across the street, with parked cars smashed by falling debris. The cause of the explosion was not immediately clear, but local media said a gas leak was suspected.

articles.title: Patriot production in Europe: Germany seeks US nod to make PAC-3 missiles
articles.summary: Germany is seeking US approval to manufacture advanced Patriot air-defence interceptors on its own soil, as rising demand and depleted stocks put pressure
articles.body: Germany is seeking US approval to manufacture advanced Patriot air-defence interceptors on its own soil, as rising demand and depleted stocks put pressure on the global supply of the missiles.According to Defense News, German defence minister Boris Pistorius said Germany has offered to manufacture US weapons in Europe, including Patriot interceptors, as part of efforts to expand defence production and ease pressure on American manufacturers.The proposal follows a Germany-US agreement aimed at allowing additional production of US weapons in Germany.Pistorius said Germany could potentially produce PAC-3 MSE and PAC-2 GEM-T interceptors, as well as other components of the Patriot system, including launchers.Germany already has experience in the Patriot supply chain. MBDA Germany is involved in producing PAC-2 interceptors, while Lockheed Martin manufactures the more advanced PAC-3 MSE. Berlin now wants to expand that industrial role to help increase overall production capacity.Patriot shortageThe push to expand Patriot production comes as the US faces a sharp depletion of its interceptor stockpile following heavy use during the Iran conflict.The shortage is particularly significant because Patriot interceptors are also needed by US forces and allies in Europe and the Middle East, while Ukraine has been using the system extensively to counter Russian missile attacks.A US defence official and a Nato official told the Associated Press in August that Patriot stocks among American and Nato forces in Europe had reached a "beyond critical" level.At the same time, replenishing the stockpile is not an immediate process. Defense News reported that CSIS estimates the production timeline for a PAC-3 MSE interceptor at around 42 months.Lockheed Martin, which manufactures the PAC-3 MSE, has said annual production capacity is being increased from around 600 interceptors to 2,000, with the 2,000-per-year target expected by the end of 2030.

articles.title: China is taking the fight to the stars. America must reclaim space supremacy
articles.summary: The People's Republic of China now holds space preeminence as the U.S. confirms on-orbit weapons and prepares for cislunar military challenges.
articles.body: As one who has had the honor to consult for NASA and the Space Shuttle team in the past; work space-defense-related issues in the Pentagon; speak with all 12 men who walked on the Moon; and author tens of columns on the subject, I have been "Johnny One-Note" over the last decade or so warning that the People’s Republic of China is seeking to establish itself as the dominant military power in space for decades to come. Did anyone in authority care? Not so much. That may now be changing. Two recent stories in the news have certainly elevated not only interest, but apprehension. The first one being when Air Force Secretary Troy Meink recently confirmed that the U.S. has weapons stationed in Earth orbit. Said Meink, in part, presumably as a warning to China and, to a lesser extent, Russia at the Air, Space and Cyber Conference: "Today, we continue to ensure we remain ready to meet the challenges of evolving threats wherever they exist. This is why the United States now has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the Joint Force against hostile adversary action…" PENTAGON REVEALS SECRET SPACE WEAPONS ARE ALREADY IN ORBIT — BUT WON'T SAY WHAT THEY DO The second — and potentially much more intriguing — was highlighted on the site "Defense One" via the headline: "The Pentagon must prepare for battles around the moon: Joint Chiefs chair." During the same Air, Space and Cyber conference in which he delivered the Keynote address, it was reported that General Dan Caine — who is the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff — said in part: "Our task, my friends, is to adapt right now, so the Joint Force is prepared to fight, endure and win in global contested environments, from the seabed to cislunar space…" NASA ANNOUNCES THREE NEW MOON MISSIONS AS AGENCY RACES TO BUILD PERMANENT LUNAR BASE BY END OF 2026 "Cislunar" in this case means not just in lunar orbit, but on the surface of the moon. The stuff of fiction? In the past, yes. Today, it must all be about the national and economic security of our nation. On that fiction front, several years ago I authored a novel — based on some real-world information from a Soviet General — titled "The Dawn of a Nazi Moon." While hopefully an entertaining and historically accurate story, the major premise of the book was to outline how an adversary could use the Moon as the ultimate "High Ground" against an enemy on Earth. The belief by some that once humans cut through Earth’s atmosphere into the vacuum of space, our flaws, greed, prejudices and military ambitions will be left behind is not only naïve, but quite dangerous. No one understood that better at the time than President John F. Kennedy. During his now iconic speech at Rice University on September 12, 1962, on the need for the U.S. to become the "preeminent spacefaring nation," President John F. Kennedy rightfully stressed in part: TRUMP TO HONOR ARTEMIS II ASTRONAUTS WHO TRAVELED FARTHER FROM EARTH THAN ANY HUMANS IN HISTORY "We mean to be a part of it — we mean to lead it. For the eyes of the world now look into space, to the Moon and to the planets beyond, and we have vowed that we shall not see it governed by a hostile flag of conquest, but by a banner of freedom and peace… Whether it will become a force for good or ill depends on man, and only if the United States occupies a position of preeminence can we help decide whether this new ocean will be a sea of peace or a new terrifying theater of war." Thanks to Kennedy, the United States did once occupy "a position of preeminence" in space. But no more. China now holds that title. TRUMP SIGNS ORDER CREATING NEW SPACE ACADEMY AKIN TO WEST POINT; ITS LOCATION WILL BE DETERMINED A China — with its entirely military-controlled space program — which is targeting all our satellites in low and geosynchronous orbit. Satellites that control the fate of our military, our economy and our nation. But much more alarmingly, it is also a China which is taking dead aim at the Moon. Both for its own military ambitions and for the future energy and economic security of its nation. One way it is doing so is by targeting the helium-3 that litters the surface of the Moon. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Helium-3 is an isotope which could provide a potentially limitless supply of safe, clean, green energy. Some experts estimate the Moon’s surface holds millions of metric tons of helium-3, and that just 25 metric tons could fuel America’s energy needs for a year. China is not waiting to find out. Via its lunar landers, it has already returned samples of helium-3 to its laboratories to be studied. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP China has every intention of conquering near-space for its military and economic needs. It appears the United States is now waking up to that power-shifting reality. And not a moment too soon. CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM DOUGLAS MACKINNON

articles.title: Why are Italian lady politicians posting photos in miniskirts? Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani’s ‘women in long skirts make better mothers’ remarks spark protest in Italy
articles.summary: Photos of female Italian politicians in miniskirts have drawn attention after comments by Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani about
articles.body: Photos of female Italian politicians in miniskirts have drawn attention after comments by Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani about what kind of woman a man should marry. The controversy began after Tajani spoke at a party political event in Formello near Rome. While discussing the kind of woman he would advise his son to marry, he contrasted a glamorous woman with a “less flashy” and “more reliable” one. Tajani said he would recommend a woman who would be “a good mother” and remain faithful, adding that she might be someone who “wears skirts that are a bit longer”. His comments were followed by criticism from opposition politicians and a protest in the Italian Senate, where female opposition senators appeared in short skirts.What did Antonio Tajani say about women and long skirts?Tajani was speaking about marriage and the advice he would give his son. According to ANSA, he said that while a glamorous woman might initially seem attractive, he would prefer a “less flashy but more reliable, more serious” woman who would be a good mother and remain faithful. He then asked whether people would prefer the glamorous woman or the more serious type, “the one who perhaps wears skirts that are a bit longer than the other's?”As reported by The Independent, Tajani also described the woman he considered more suitable for marriage as “perhaps less pretty, with a slightly longer skirt”. He linked this choice to stability and fidelity in marriage. His comments quickly became a subject of political criticism, with opponents questioning the idea that clothing could be connected with a woman's reliability or suitability as a wife or mother.Why did women politicians wear miniskirts to the Italian Senate?On September 22, a group of female opposition senators appeared together in short skirts at Italy's Senate in response to Tajani's remarks. The protest included politicians from opposition groups including the Democratic Party, Five Star Movement, Italia Viva and the Greens and Left Alliance. The initiative was proposed by Italia Viva senator Raffaella Paita. Paita explained the protest as a statement about freedom of dress. “This is a gesture of freedom to say that we are free to dress however we want,” she said. The protest also became a direct visual response to Tajani's reference to skirt length as part of his example about choosing a wife.Chiara Appendino posted a miniskirt photoFormer Turin mayor and Five Star Movement MP Chiara Appendino was among the politicians who responded publicly. She posted a photograph on Facebook of herself in a miniskirt and directly addressed Tajani. “Tajani, am I not a ‘trustworthy’ woman? Am I not a ‘good mother’?” she asked. She added: “We cannot allow a minister in 2026 to tell us that we should marry a woman who wears longer skirts and is less showy.” Politician Fiorella Zabatta, spokesperson for the opposition Greens and Left Alliance, also criticised Tajani's comments. “Tajani isn’t decades behind the times, he’s thousands of years behind,” she said. She also called on the government to focus on women who have been killed rather than judging the clothing of women who are alive. “Count the women who have been killed before measuring the skirt lengths of those who are alive,” Zabatta said. Her comments came amid a wider debate in Italy over women's safety and political discussion around women's rights.Tajani apologisesTajani later apologised for the remarks. Speaking in New York on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly, he said: “I apologise if anyone was offended by what I said, but I never intended to offend women.” The apology came after several days of criticism over his original comments. The Senate protest turned Tajani's comments about skirt length into a visual political statement. Instead of debating whether a long or short skirt indicated anything about a woman's character, the opposition senators used their clothing to make the opposite point: that women can choose what they wear without that choice determining how they should be viewed as wives, mothers or public figures.You use AI every day. articles.title: Switzerland’s neutrality vote is asking the wrong question
articles.summary: The real question is what neutrality can still do for Switzerland.
articles.body:
On September 27, Switzerland votes on whether to lock a stricter definition of neutrality into its constitution. The initiative would bar Switzerland from cooperating with a military alliance unless it were under military attack or such an attack were being prepared, and prevent it from imposing sanctions on a belligerent state unless those sanctions were mandated by the United Nations Security Council (UNSC). Polls suggest it will fail, with 63 percent intending to reject it. But that result says less about Swiss faith in neutrality — which remains overwhelming — than about how badly the vote and the surrounding debates miss the real issue: the vote asks whether to restrict sanctions and alliances; the real question is how neutrality can still deliver security and prosperity.

Neutrality has shaped Swiss identity since 1815, when the European powers recognised Switzerland’s permanent neutrality after the Napoleonic Wars. It survived two world wars and the Cold War on a basic premise: keeping foreign armies off Swiss territory would keep Switzerland out of other countries’ wars, while trading with all sides would keep its diverse economy connected to the markets on which its welfare depends.

The neutrality initiative grew out of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Switzerland had adopted European Union sanctions before, but sanctioning Russia specifically — a major power Switzerland had long sought not to antagonise — cut deeper. It sharpened a question earlier cases had already raised: whether economic measures against a belligerent power were compatible with neutrality at all. The Swiss People’s Party and Pro Schweiz, or Pro Suisse, launched the initiative to preserve the stricter model they believed had served Switzerland well.

A “yes” vote would bring significant changes, while a “no” would largely mean a continuation of the flexible, case-by-case neutrality Switzerland practises today. A “yes” could force Switzerland to unwind its existing sanctions against Russia and would prevent it from joining future EU- or United States-led sanctions against belligerent states unless those sanctions were mandated by the UNSC. It would also constrain the bilateral cyber, air-defence and joint-exercise cooperation with its neighbours (that happen to be members of NATO) that Switzerland has expanded since 2022 — precisely the kind of cooperation it may need more of as the European security environment deteriorates. But whichever way Switzerland votes, the harder questions will remain, because the initiative answers a 2022 question, and the world has moved on in three ways it cannot address.

Three things have changed since 2022: the nature of the threat from Russia, the reliability of the US as a trading partner and the strategic implications of China’s economic weight.

The first is the threat itself. For two centuries, Swiss neutrality was designed primarily to protect its security in the context of a territorial war. Switzerland, a heavily armed state in the Alps, made invasion costly and denied foreign armies an easy route through Swiss territory. That model has much less to say about a new threat: a European war that indirectly yet significantly affects Switzerland.

Switzerland’s 2026 Security Policy Strategy warns of a “window of vulnerability” emerging in Europe around 2028 as Russia rebuilds military capacity while Europe rearms. In such a conflict, Switzerland could face missiles or drones crossing its airspace without knowing immediately who launched them or where they are headed. Switzerland is also deeply integrated into Europe’s financial, rail, electricity and data networks. A continental conflict would therefore reach it even if no foreign soldier crossed its border.

Russian hostility towards Switzerland has also increased since 2022. In 2024, Swiss authorities uncovered an alleged Russian effort to obtain sensitive military-related material in Switzerland. Cyberattacks also targeted Swiss government websites around the Ukraine peace summit that June. By 2025, Swiss intelligence was warning that the country faced growing risks of espionage, sabotage and operations involving critical infrastructure, specifically from Russia. Whether that hostility is payback for Switzerland’s sanctions or simply reflects Russia’s broader confrontation with Europe matters less than the practical conclusion: formal neutrality does not guarantee security, and security cannot be obtained in isolation.

The second change is US foreign and trade policy. In 2022, Switzerland could still assume a relatively stable relationship with its major trading partners. That is harder now. In 2025, Washington imposed a 39 percent tariff on many Swiss exports. The shock and disbelief remain, even after the tariff was reduced to 15 percent following negotiations and major Swiss investment commitments. The episode showed that neutral status buys no economic goodwill: Washington’s trade policy is driven by its own interests, not by Switzerland’s neutrality. And if neutrality cannot shield Switzerland from a partner’s tariffs, abstaining from sanctions will not shield it either. For Bern, the practical response should therefore be not stricter neutrality but greater economic diversification.

That makes China more important. Swiss-Chinese goods trade is worth more than 50 billion Swiss francs ($60.4bn) a year when gold is included, while trade with Russia was 4.7 billion francs in 2021, the last full year before the invasion, when Russia ranked 23rd among Switzerland’s trading partners. Bern and Beijing are also deepening their free-trade relationship, with negotiations on an upgraded agreement concluded in August 2026 that would make 99.8 percent of current Swiss exports to China tariff-free. Sanctioning China in a future crisis over Taiwan would therefore impose costs on Switzerland on an entirely different scale from sanctions against Moscow.

Ironically, both sides of the neutrality debate may eventually reach the same conclusion: supporters of stricter neutrality would oppose such sanctions on principle, their opponents on economic grounds. That convergence is the point. If Switzerland’s answer to the next great-power crisis is the same whichever way it votes on September 27, the constitution is not where the real decision is being made. The initiative regulates what Switzerland does — whom it joins and whom it sanctions. The new threats depend on what others do to Switzerland, whatever its posture.

Three questions will outlast the vote. The first is how closely Switzerland should cooperate with its neighbours, including NATO members, without undermining the credibility of neutrality. Modern air defence depends increasingly on shared radar, intelligence and coordination across borders. Switzerland’s accession to the European Sky Shield Initiative in 2024 is the live example. Switzerland argues that such cooperation can take place in peacetime without creating an alliance.

The deeper that cooperation becomes, however, the harder the distinction may be to sustain in the eyes of a potential adversary. Too little cooperation could leave Swiss airspace vulnerable; too much could make Switzerland appear functionally aligned with NATO. Neutrality depends not only on legal definitions but also on how other states interpret Swiss behaviour.

The second question is whether Switzerland can close its military capabilities gap fast enough for neutrality to remain credible. Defence spending fell from 1.4 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 1990 to 0.7 percent by 2021 and is set to reach only 1 percent by 2032 — still four years after Switzerland’s own warning of a “window of vulnerability” from around 2028. That gap matters: a country unable to defend its territory and airspace becomes dependent on its neighbours in a crisis, reducing the freedom of action neutrality is meant to preserve.

Nor is this only a defence question: the 1907 Hague Conventions oblige a neutral state to prevent belligerents from using its territory, while armed neutrality requires Switzerland to be able to defend that territory, so the capability gap is a neutrality problem in its own right. Real deterrence, not constitutional wording, is what makes neutrality credible.

The third question is how much taking sides costs, and when. The current debate often conflates the legal requirements of armed neutrality with the morality of foreign policy: whether Switzerland can legally condemn or sanction a specific aggressor becomes mixed with whether it has a moral obligation to do so in every case, with too little attention paid to how the consequences differ in peace and war. In peacetime, being perceived as partial may weaken Switzerland’s credibility and value as a mediator — a meaningful but ultimately manageable cost. In wartime, the consequences could be far more serious. If an adversary regards Switzerland as effectively aligned with its enemy, the country could lose much of the practical protection neutrality is meant to provide while still lacking the guarantees of a formal alliance. That would leave it with the worst of both worlds: treated as aligned by an adversary, without allies obliged to defend it.

The referendum outcome therefore risks turning a strategic problem into a legal one. Switzerland certainly needs to decide what neutrality means in the 21st century. But the decisive questions concern deterrence, defence cooperation, economic vulnerability and credibility, not simply whether sanctions and alliances should be restricted in the constitution.

Neutrality was never really the question. What Switzerland can still achieve with it is.

articles.title: In 1995, Galápagos crews began clearing goats and burros from Alcedo Volcano; after 62,868 goats vanished by 2006, juvenile tortoises and growth rates increased
articles.summary: The successful eradication of 62,868 feral goats from Alcedo Volcano in the Galápagos Islands has resulted in significant growth in the juvenile giant tortoise population and improved overall health of the species, as revealed by recent research.
articles.body: A goat eradication campaign on Alcedo Volcano in the Galápagos removed 62,868 animals by 2006, and researchers who were tracking the island’s giant tortoises found changes in the population as the goats disappeared. The proportion of juvenile tortoises increased, while individual tortoises also recorded higher growth rates during the later stages of the eradication campaign. The findings came from long-term monitoring that was carried out alongside the effort to remove the introduced animals.The campaign began in 1995 against feral goats and burros on Alcedo Volcano, where the animals had become a major pressure on the native ecosystem, and the giant tortoise population was one of the main reasons for the eradication effort. The study was published in Restoration Ecology, and compared tortoise data from earlier and later stages of the campaign and also looked at a control population on nearby Santa Cruz Island, where goats and donkeys were not removed.The researchers found that the proportion of juveniles among the Alcedo tortoises increased as the eradication progressed, and individual tortoises also grew faster during the later period. In Santa Cruz, where the introduced animals remained, researchers did not see the same changes in juvenile proportions or individual growth rates.Finding the goats that were left behindConservation teams had to find animals that had become increasingly difficult to locate across northern Isabela’s terrain as the population declined. Project Isabela used sterilized goats fitted with radio collars, known as “Judas goats,” to do that. Goats are social animals, which is why the released animals sought out other goats and joined them. Rangers could then track the Judas goats by radio telemetry and locate the remaining feral animals. Galápagos Conservancy says about 770 Judas goats were eventually used on Isabela. Helicopters were also used for aerial hunting and tracking, while GIS technology helped teams map their work.The goats had changed Alcedo's vegetationGalápagos Conservancy says that goats reached northern Isabela after being introduced elsewhere on the island and eventually expanded into the Alcedo area. Their grazing had damaged forests and vegetation that provided food and water resources for giant tortoises by the early 1990s.Project Isabela officially began in 1997 after an international workshop produced a plan for eliminating introduced mammals from northern Isabela, Santiago and Pinta. Northern Isabela was declared goat-free in 2006, although monitoring continued with a small number of Judas goats. Galápagos Conservancy reports that small trees regenerated from stumps that were left by grazing, while highland shrubs, forest seedlings, Opuntia cactus and other endemic plants increased. Some species that had survived only in protected craters or fenced areas were also found expanding as grazing pressure fell. Alcedo is home to one of the Galápagos' major giant tortoise populations, and they depend on vegetation for food and use parts of the volcano's highlands during the island's dry periods.The eradication period overlapped with a rare climatic event that increased forage availability, but the researchers noted that the nearby control population on Santa Cruz did not show comparable changes. Their analysis therefore identified goat and burro removal as the primary cause of the improvement in the Alcedo tortoise population status.The animals that had altered the volcano's vegetation were gone, while monitoring of the native tortoises had documented measurable changes in the population by 2006. The eradication became part of the larger restoration of northern Isabela, where introduced mammals had altered habitats that were occupied by native species for decades.You use AI every day. articles.title: US backs Elon Musk's bid to overturn €120m EU fine against X
articles.summary: The EU had said X "deceives users" by selling blue ticks without "meaningfully verifying" accounts.
articles.body:
The US government is seeking to join Elon Musk's legal challenge to overturn a €120m (£105m) EU fine against X over its blue tick badges.

In December 2025, the European Commission said the platform "deceives users" by allowing people to pay for a blue verified check mark, because it is not "meaningfully verifying" who is behind the account.

But US Assistant Attorney General Brett A. Shumate said on Thursday that the commission had "inappropriately attempted" to expand its reach to American companies outside its control.

Musk, who spent millions helping elect Donald Trump and other Republicans, has previously claimed EU tech regulation "inhibits progress" for companies.

The US Department of Justice (DOJ) has filed an application with the EU's General Court in support of Musk's and X's attempts to dismiss ​the case.

It claims that under a section of law in the Statute of the Court of Justice of the EU, a state may intervene in disputes before the court if it "can establish an interest in the result of the case to the court".

The DOJ said the US "has a clear interest" in ensuring any decision by the commission was applied consistently with "how territorial jurisdiction is generally understood in international law".

It also wants to make sure it would not "otherwise prejudice" US-headquartered digital services that "contribute significantly" to its economy.

In a press briefing on Friday , European Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier said it was "ready to defend" its position in court.

He added that the commission had an "solid case" at its disposal, due to the alleged breach of its Digital Services Act.

In addition to its use of blue ticks, EU regulators had accused X of failing to provide transparency around its adverts and denying researchers access to public data.

Henna Virkkunen, the regulator's executive vice-president for tech sovereignty, said at the time of the fine's issue it was "holding X responsible for undermining users' rights and evading accountability".

"Deceiving users with blue checkmarks, obscuring information on ads and shutting out researchers have no place online in the EU," she said.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) had criticised the EU regulator, accusing it of attacking and censoring US firms.

"The European Commission's fine isn't just an attack on X, it's an attack on all American tech platforms and the American people by foreign governments," Rubio wrote in a post on X.

"The days of censoring Americans online are over."

His remarks were reposted by Musk, who added "absolutely".

The European Commission denied targeting any specific nationality, stating it is simply protecting its digital and democratic standards to maintain its role as a global benchmark.

The action marked the Commission's first official non-compliance decision under the Digital Services Act (DSA), one of two mandatory rulebooks governing online platforms in the EU.

However, the EU is also conducting several other investigations into the platform, including one into its integrated AI assistant Grok over concerns it was used to create sexualised images of real people.

articles.title: Japan says Trump voiced concern over weak yen in summit with PM Takaichi
articles.summary: President Donald Trump raised concern about yen weakness during a summit with Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, Japan’s Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama said, offering an unusually detailed account of the leaders’ talks on currencies.
articles.body: President Donald Trump raised concern about yen weakness during a summit with Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, Japan’s Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama said, offering an unusually detailed account of the leaders’ talks on currencies. “At the recent Japan-US summit meeting, President Trump expressed concern about the yen’s weakness,” Katayama said at a regular news conference, adding that she was disclosing the exchange for the first time after consulting with the Prime Minister’s Office. “Prime Minister Takaichi told him, as a general principle, that an undervalued yen is problematic,” Katayama said. Katayama’s unusually frank account of leaders’ talks, which governments typically keep confidential, points to shared concern in Tokyo and Washington over the yen’s continued slide despite their joint intervention in July. Takaichi met Trump in New York on Tuesday on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly. She later told reporters they had a “timely” discussion about China ahead of Trump’s planned summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping. Katayama said the leaders’ discussion on foreign exchange reaffirmed the shared US-Japan stance behind their July 31 coordinated intervention, including a commitment to counter excessive volatility and disorderly moves in the yen. “In light of this summit meeting, Treasury Secretary (Scott) Bessent and I will continue to communicate closely on a range of matters, including foreign exchange,” she said. The dollar has been rallying against the yen and other major currencies, driven by strong US economic data, a hawkish Federal Reserve and surging US bond yields. The yen strengthened slightly after Katayama’s remarks, rising from 158.60 per dollar to trade at around 158. The weak yen is driving up energy import costs that are already elevated due to the US-Israeli war on Iran, fueling concerns about an inflation overshoot, a headache for Japanese policymakers and for the US, which is worried that a selloff in Japanese bonds could spill over into the Treasury market. Katayama declined to comment on whether global rises in government bond yields were discussed at the Japan-US summit. The benchmark 10-year Japanese government bond yield jumped to a 30-year high of 3.115% on Friday following a steep selloff in the US market. At a separate news conference, Minoru Kiuchi, the minister in charge of economic revitalization and an ally of Takaichi’s reflationist camp, said the phase of Abenomics-style reflation policies, with monetary easing and agile fiscal spending, is over. Kiuchi’s remarks appeared to respond to comments from Bessent, who recently suggested that Japan’s priority should be fighting inflation rather than stimulating growth, signaling concern about what he sees as lingering elements of Abenomics in Takaichi’s policies and among her political allies. Hirofumi Suzuki, chief FX strategist at Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corp, said remarks by both Katayama and Kiuchi reflected a heightened sense of concern over the yen’s weakness, particularly after Tokyo conducted rate checks on Friday, a move that is often viewed as a precursor to currency intervention.

articles.title: Iran pitches seven-day roadmap to end conflict with US
articles.summary: Tehran seeks rapid implementation failed ceasefire deal, offering to open Hormuz if regional conflicts halted.
articles.body:
Iran has proposed a seven-day roadmap aimed at ending the war with the United States.

Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi outlined the plan to reporters in New York on Thursday, according to US media. The proposal seeks to implement the conditions in the Memorandum of Understanding agreed by Washington and Tehran in June, including a halt to hostilities and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.

Reportedly passed to Washington via mediators earlier this week, Iran’s proposal asks the US to meet specific conditions within seven days to restart ceasefire talks and end the blockade choking the strategically important strait.

The restrictions on maritime traffic in Hormuz have become a key issue in the conflict due to the impact on oil and gas exports and the global economy.

The proposal, which was presented to reporters on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly, comes as the war, started by US and Israeli strikes, is almost into its seventh month.

The US-Iran MoU deal expired in August as each side accused the other of violations, and there has been little sign since that they could return to the agreement, although Tehran has suggested it could happen.

Under Iran’s proposal, hostilities would end on all fronts, including Gaza and Lebanon, within seven days, The New York Times reported.

Washington would also release Iran’s frozen assets, estimated at no less than $12bn, waive sanctions on Iranian oil and lift its naval blockade.

The Strait of Hormuz would reopen on the final day of the period. Talks on Iran’s nuclear programme, ostensibly the root cause of the conflict according to President Donald Trump, would start immediately.

The proposal closely resembles the MoU, but sets out a hugely ambitious timetable. The Pakistani and Qatari-brokered deal signed on June 17 set a 60-day window for negotiations, but still unravelled within weeks.

Vague wording led to disputes over who controlled shipping through the strait, and the two sides traded attacks before US President Donald Trump declared the deal “over” on July 7 .

Earlier this month, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Tehran would “immediately reciprocate” if the US returned to its commitments under the MoU.

“We have introduced a plan to the United States through the intermediators,” Araghchi told reporters.

An unnamed White House official told CNN that the administration was having “positive and constructive discussions through the mediators”. The New York Times quoted an official as saying that Washington would not rush into a deal.

An Iranian security source told Al Jazeera there could be room for further diplomatic engagement if Washington met Iran’s conditions and commitments.

However, analysts said the proposal suggests that diplomatic efforts between the US and Iran are not advancing significantly.

“Basically nothing has really changed,” Cyrus Schayegh, professor of international history and politics at the Geneva Graduate Institute, told Al Jazeera.

Iran “keeps insisting that it wants to keep the additional power it gained during the war and that the June memorandum still is basically key to the roadmap moving forward,” said the professor, while the US “keeps basically refusing to accept this roadmap debate”.

No significant movement towards ending the conflict is likely before the US mid-term elections in November, he asserted.

Araghchi told reporters that “it would be better” to reach a deal before that vote. Pezeshkian said earlier that any agreements with the US would not be tied to the timing of the midterms, according to CNN.

Qatar’s Foreign Ministry said on Friday that top diplomat Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, one of the main mediators in the conflicts across the Middle East region, had spoken with Pezeshkian about de-escalation and conditions for dialogue.

articles.title: In 2023, a 94-year-old Minnesota woman lost her condo over about $2,300 in taxes; the county kept roughly $25,000 until the Supreme Court stepped in
articles.summary: In a significant legal victory, the US Supreme Court ruled that Hennepin County could not keep surplus proceeds from the sale of Geraldine Tyler's condo, which was seized for unpaid taxes. This case highlights the long-standing property rights of homeowners and has implications for tax foreclosure practices across the United States.
articles.body: A property tax bill of roughly $2,300 eventually cost Geraldine Tyler far more than the amount she owed. The 94-year-old Minnesota woman lost her Minneapolis condominium after unpaid taxes, interest and penalties accumulated over several years. According to the US Supreme Court, Hennepin County sold the property for $40,000 and kept the money left after settling Tyler's tax debt. In 2023, the dispute reached the Supreme Court, which ruled that the government could not keep the surplus value of her home. Tyler's case became an important test of what happens when a government takes property to recover an unpaid tax bill. The dispute was not over whether the county could collect the taxes, but whether it could keep more than Tyler owed.How the tax debt grewThe U.S. Supreme Court also noted that Tyler purchased a one-bedroom condo in Minneapolis in 1999 and lived there for many years. As she aged, she moved to a senior living facility in 2010. She continued to own the condo after moving out, but the property taxes went unpaid. By 2015, the original tax liability of about $2,300 had grown to roughly $15,000 with interest and penalties. Hennepin County then took ownership of the condo under Minnesota’s tax-forfeiture system and sold it for $40,000, enough to cover the outstanding debt.A later William & Mary Law Review article examined Tyler’s case in the broader context of tax-foreclosure practices and the loss of home equity when governments sell homes for unpaid taxes. Tyler challenged the arrangement in court, arguing that keeping the surplus violated the Fifth Amendment's Takings Clause, which prevents the government from taking private property for public use without just compensation. She also raised a claim under the Eighth Amendment's Excessive Fines Clause. Her case initially failed. A federal district court dismissed it, and the US Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit upheld that decision. The appellate court reasoned that Minnesota law did not recognise Tyler's right to the surplus proceeds after the forfeiture. The Supreme Court later agreed to hear the case.What the Supreme Court decidedAccording to the Legal Information Institute, the Supreme Court unanimously ruled in Tyler v. Hennepin County on May 25, 2023. Chief Justice John Roberts, writing for the Court, said the county could take Tyler's property to satisfy the tax debt but could not use that debt as a basis for taking additional value belonging to her. The Court pointed to a long history of property law recognising an owner's interest in the value remaining after a government debt has been satisfied. It also noted that Minnesota itself had historically recognised a homeowner's right to surplus proceeds before changing its law in 1935.A ruling with consequences beyond one condoThe impact of the case went beyond Tyler’s one-bedroom condo. The Supreme Court’s decision brought more attention to what happens when a property is worth far more than the taxes owed on it. In Minnesota, the ruling led to guidance for counties on dealing with extra money left over after tax-forfeiture sales, as well as changes and further discussion around the state’s tax-forfeiture rules.The decision did not mean governments could no longer collect unpaid property taxes or take action against properties with outstanding debts. Instead, it focused on what happens after the debt has been covered. In Tyler’s case, the county was entitled to recover what it was owed, but the court found that keeping the remaining value of the property raised a separate constitutional question.You use AI every day.
