articles.title: FAQs on Section 138 of NI Act: What happens once your cheque is dishonoured?
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: A bounced cheque feels like a banking hassle, but legally it can be a criminal offence.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A bounced cheque feels like a banking hassle, but legally it can be a criminal offence. Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 can turn a dishonoured cheque into a court case and, for some, a jail sentence.What is Section 138?Section 138 deals with a cheque being returned unpaid because there is not enough money in the account or because the amount is more than the arrangement made with the bank.If a person issues a cheque towards a legally enforceable debt and the cheque is returned unpaid for these reasons, the person who issued the cheque can face legal proceedings, but only if the conditions set by law are met.Section 138 was added only in 1988. The original 1881 Act did not have any punishment for cheque bounce.When does a bounced cheque actually become an offence?A bounced cheque does not automatically become an offence.The cheque must have been issued for a genuine debt, presented within its three-month validity period and returned unpaid specifically because there was not enough money in the account or because the amount exceeded the arrangement with the bank.The person receiving the cheque must also follow the legal procedure after the cheque is dishonoured.What must the payee do after the cheque is dishonoured?The payee must send a written demand notice to the person who issued the cheque within 30 days of learning that the cheque was dishonoured.The person who issued the cheque then gets 15 days from receiving the notice to make the payment.If the payment is not made within those 15 days, the right to file a case arises.What if the drawer pays within those 15 days?If the drawer makes the payment within the 15-day period, no offence arises on that basis.The notice is meant to give the drawer an opportunity to make the payment before facing prosecution.How much time does the payee have to file a case, and where?The complaint must be filed within one month from the date on which the right to file the case arises. The court can allow a delay in appropriate cases.The case goes before a Judicial Magistrate First Class. It is filed in the court that has jurisdiction over the bank branch where the cheque was presented for payment.What punishment can follow?A person convicted under Section 138 can face imprisonment of up to two years, a fine of up to twice the cheque amount, or both.The offence is bailable, compoundable and non-cognizable. This means that arrest is not automatic and the matter can be settled.Courts often favour compensation instead of jail, particularly when the drawer offers to make the payment with interest.Can the case be settled before trial?Yes. Section 147 allows the parties to settle the case at any stage, even after a complaint has been filed.Can the complainant get money while the case is pending?Sometimes. Section 143A, added in 2018, allows the trial court to order the drawer to pay interim compensation of up to 20 percent of the cheque amount once the accused pleads not guilty or after charges are framed.This is not automatic. It is up to the court to decide whether such compensation should be ordered. If the drawer is later acquitted, the complainant has to return the amount with interest.What if the cheque was issued by a company?Section 141 extends liability to company officers, but this does not happen automatically.Courts require evidence showing that the dishonour was connected to the specific director's conduct or consent. For example, a retired director will not be liable for a cheque that bounced after the director had left the company unless their involvement is shown.Does every bounced cheque lead to a conviction?No. The person who filed the complaint must prove all the required elements, and the drawer can raise defences.The law does presume, under Section 139, that a cheque was received towards repayment of a genuine debt. But this presumption can be challenged with evidence, so it does not guarantee a conviction on its own.Can someone be arrested right after a cheque bounces?No. The payee must first complete the notice process and then approach the court. Since the offence is non-cognizable, there is no direct arrest without going through this process.Is this a civil or criminal matter?It is a criminal matter. However, the proceedings also effectively involve recovery of the cheque amount, and courts can consider compensation depending on the stage of the case.What if someone convicted wants to appeal?Section 148 allows the appellate court to require a deposit of at least 20 percent of the fine or compensation as a condition for hearing the appeal.TakeawayDates are particularly important in cheque dishonour cases because the law sets specific time limits for the notice and for filing the complaint.Section 138 does not make every bounced cheque a criminal offence automatically. It applies only when its conditions are met.For payees, the key steps are cheque dishonour, sending the notice within the required time, giving the drawer 15 days to make the payment and filing the complaint within the prescribed time.For drawers, ignoring a notice can lead to prosecution. At the same time, the law allows settlement, recovery and genuine defences during the proceedings.

articles.title: 'Media coverage is important': Pope Leo XIV backs press freedom amid Trump-US news outlets clash
articles.summary: Pope Leo XIV on Friday defended the media’s right to cover public figures, following US President Donald Trump’s unsuccessful efforts to bar some news
articles.body: Pope Leo XIV on Friday defended the media’s right to cover public figures, following US President Donald Trump’s unsuccessful efforts to bar some news outlets critical of his administration from the White House.The pope spoke to reporters aboard the papal plane en route to France for a four-day visit. Asked by a CNN reporter about the Trump administration’s efforts to bar the network and two other media houses, Leo replied the media was welcome aboard his plane.“I am very happy that everyone is welcome here. Good media coverage is important, and it is equally important that we have it all the way around, for everyone,” said Leo, the first American to become pope.CNN, MS NOW and Politico returned to the White House on Thursday after a judge temporarily blocked Trump’s ban on the outlets. But the dispute between the president and news organisations whose coverage he dislikes continued.On a high-profile day, as Chinese leader Xi Jinping visited Washington and attended a state dinner, no major US television network aired live coverage. CNN and MS NOW also claimed their journalists were denied access to Xi’s arrival at the state dinner.Pope Leo XIV apologises to pressLeo has repeatedly affirmed the importance of a free and independent press, including in one of his first audiences as pope. Speaking to journalists who covered the 2025 conclave that elected him, he had called for the release of imprisoned journalists and described free speech and a free press as a “precious gift.”During the flight to France, Leo also apologised for missing an opportunity to speak with reporters during his previous international trip. At the time, his Iberia charter aircraft broke down in Spain’s Canary Islands, forcing him to return to the Vatican alone aboard the Spanish king’s private jet and miss the traditional airborne press conference.More than 70 reporters and members of the Vatican delegation waited for several hours at the airport for a replacement aircraft. Leo addressed their disappointment when he went to the back of the plane to greet them.“A special mention I would like to make for those of you who were travelling with me when we returned to Rome from Spain,” he said. “I want to apologise personally for an incident that I had nothing to do with, but which I know left a number of you unhappy because we couldn’t make the flight back to Rome together.”(With AP inputs)You use AI every day. articles.title: Ridiculed MSP says chest infection and lack of sleep led to committee blunder
articles.summary: Collette Stevenson says she has faced "misogynistic bullying" after asking whether government agency Transport Scotland is a charity.
articles.body:
An MSP who faced ridicule over a blunder at a Holyrood committee has said she suffered a "momentary lapse" brought on by lack of sleep and a chest infection.

Collette Stevenson, who has represented East Kilbride for the SNP since 2021 and is a member of the transport committee, was criticised after asking if Transport Scotland was a registered charity.

Transport Scotland director Graeme Cook then explained to her that it was a national agency which was part of the Scottish government.

Posting on Facebook, Stevenson said her illness had affected her concentration, and said she had been subjected to "misogynistic bullying" following the incident.

The 57-year-old added that she later took a week off work, on medical advice, to recuperate.

She posted: "During a recent committee evidence session, I experienced a momentary lapse in my questioning regarding the status of Transport Scotland.

"I was in the early stages of a severe chest infection, which affected my sleep and, in turn, my concentration.

"On medical advice, and following a flare up of asthma, I have taken this week off from Parliament to recuperate and allow the various medications to work, so I can focus on making a full recovery."

Stevenson sits on the equality, human rights and civil justice committee as well as the transport committee, and is a substitute member of the delegated powers and law reform committee.

She has previously asked questions during committee meetings about the Clyde Metro development - a key recommendation from Transport Scotland's strategic transport review - and worked with the body on the East Kilbride rail enhancement and electrification project.

But earlier this month, after about two hours of evidence on Scotland's rail services, Stevenson asked: "I take it Transport Scotland is a registered charity?"

"Transport Scotland is a non-departmental government body," Graeme Cook, director of rail delivery for Transport Scotland, responded.

"Transport Scotland is an agency so all of the Transport Scotland staff are already part of the civil service.

"Transport Scotland is the same legal entity as the Scottish government."

Stevenson said that since her mistake she had been ridiculed and bullied online.

She said: "Whilst robust scrutiny is a necessary part of public life, the disproportionate abuse, mockery, and misogynistic bullying directed at me online following an honest mistake demonstrates the toxic culture women in politics still have to endure far too often."

The MSP added her focus remained on serving her community, and thanked her friends, colleagues and constituents for their kindness and support.

After the incident, SNP minister Stephen Gethins stood up for Stevenson's character, describing her as "a really good colleague and fantastic local advocate".

articles.title: Flood-hit Somerset farmer welcomes prevention projects
articles.summary: Farmer James Winslade says it is "brilliant" the council has £50m for flood prevention work.
articles.body:
A farmer who saw his land devastated by flooding has welcomed the allocation of funding towards flood prevention measures.

Somerset Council has allocated a government grant of £50m on flood prevention work, including dredging, improvements to pumping stations and flood warning systems.

James Winslade, a farmer near Burrowbridge in Somerset who saw "every bit" of the family's 900 acres underwater in 2014 , hopes the money can help prevent future disasters.

"It's brilliant to have that money. Dredging and permanent pumps mean we can get water moving a lot quicker," said Winslade, adding he was keen for work to be completed.

"The trouble is, the money hasn't been spent. Now we're catching up from lack of investment," Winslade added.

"I'd like to actually see work being done on the ground."

Winslade, whose family has farmed on the Somerset Levels for three generations, was among people who had to evacuate during the floods which made international headlines.

'AI helped diagnose my daughter's rare condition'

'I thought it was perimenopause but it was incurable cancer'

Henry superfan, 8, shows off vacuum collection

In June, the Department for Environment, Food, and Rural Affairs announced that Somerset Council would be allocated £50m for flood resilience.

Since then, the council has developed a flood resilience programme consisting of 15 projects the money will be spent on.

The first allocation will be about £650,000 for communities, emergency response, and to fund gully maintenance ahead of the coming winter.

One of the community projects is My Community, a Somerset Council programme supplying residents with home maintenance and installation of flood-resilient washing machines, toilets and showers.

Federica Smith-Roberts, Somerset Council's lead member for communities, climate change and environment, said an advisory board with people from key agencies and the community has been working on a draft programme "with the aim of moving at pace to deliver some key measures as soon as possible".

"The My Community programme will be a crucial part of this," she said.

Somerset Levels resident and flooding campaigner Bryony Sadler said: "Some of the projects that are being used I'm not in favour of.

"No matter how good your drainage system is, unless it's unblocked, that water is still going to be here and it's going to affect us and then we can't go to the shop and the railway is flooded."

Some of the funds will go to help the Internal Drainage Boards carry out additional dredging and desilting work.

And about £3m will help the Environment Agency (EA) improve existing pumping stations across Somerset.

"With winter fast approaching, we're pleased Somerset Council has confirmed that flood resilience funding will reach communities before challenging weather sets in, and we'll continue working closely with the council and partners on the programme," an EA spokesperson said.

articles.title: British Army veteran conned by AI ex-soldier's 'pity scam'
articles.summary: Raymond Gilbert paid £155 for an item he believed was handmade by a fellow British ex-serviceman.
articles.body:
Experts have warned of a growing wave of AI-generated "pity scams" using fake videos of injured ex-military personnel to sell products online.

Army veteran Raymond Gilbert, 63, from Bradenstoke, Wiltshire, said he was scammed by a TikTok account claiming to belong to a fellow ex-serviceman.

He spent £154.99 buying a "handmade" wooden flag that he said turned out to be made in China. The BBC identified 45 similar TikTok accounts, along with more on other platforms, selling military-themed items.

A TikTok spokesperson said it had strict rules against "harmfully misleading AI-generated content and scams" and that it had removed the content and accounts shared with them.

Warning as woman fined £500 for dog microchip error

Alcoholic former GP saved by Salvation Army

Chinook helicopter lands in field after bird strike

Gilbert was a quality manager for the British Army in Afghanistan, working at Camp Bastion and Kandahar.

"I was scrolling through TikTok and this guy came up who had hurt himself, working from a garage making flags to supplement his income," he said.

"I thought it was endearing, his wife was supporting him, and the final product looked good."

Gilbert said he clicked through to an external website to make his purchase.

"I checked it, and it all did look very good; there were previous sales, and everything looked kosher," he said.

When the parcel arrived, Gilbert said there was Chinese writing on the envelope, and the flag was a printed image on glued plywood.

"It is a despicable, insidious way of trying to con somebody; it's a low moral thing to do," he said.

"People need to be aware that AI is getting better and humans are getting worse."

The BBC has seen similar videos on Facebook, Instagram and YouTube, with sellers offering bags, chopping boards and door wreaths.

Many raise suspicions due to the veterans' injuries changing, stories being copied across different accounts and the videos looking professionally produced.

When asked about the claims that they were fake, one account, @ogudujona, said "these are made in London sir", but declined to give details of their regiment or time served in the forces.

Technology expert Will Guyatt said he had seen an increase in what he called "pity scam" videos online.

"The reality is these videos are made in minutes," he said.

"You can even say [to the chatbots] when you're creating them to make it more deliberately emotional.

"It's really hard to tell the difference; back in the old days these characters might have had six fingers on a hand, but now it looks almost identical to reality."

Guyatt added that dozens of bot accounts then flood the comments of the AI videos to encourage people to buy them.

Guyatt gave his tips to avoid falling for AI scams like this:

Look closely for mistakes in videos, like extra fingers or items disappearing

If it looks too good to be true, it probably is

Ask an internet savvy friend or family member

Check for the products being sold elsewhere online

Senior associate at Forbes Solicitors, Daniel Fletcher, said: "Consumers have the right to a refund, but the territorial nature of these adverts means it's difficult to actually exercise these rights.

"We're relying on these e-commerce platforms to proactively take down these adverts, but once it's taken down, the trader will create a new platform and put it back up again.

"The Advertising Standards Authority tries its best to inform consumers, but it is quite difficult to police.

"In many respects, we're fighting a bit of a losing battle."

Ex-serviceman Simon Gray, a resident at the Alabaré home in Bristol, said he was "disgusted" by the videos.

"A close friend of mine was done by an IED in Afghanistan ...I got slightly choked watching these; it looks so believable," he said.

"It's on a sick level; this will harm veterans in the long run.

"We rely on people's kindness and donations to not be sleeping on the streets."

Fellow resident Leo Dromgoole said the videos made him "angry".

"There are criminals, and then there are criminals, and people like that [making these videos] they're even further down the line," he added.

Genuine veteran charities say that scam videos using fake veterans and made-up stories of hardship could make their job harder.

Spencer Bull, from Help for Heroes, said: "It's a real shame that we've come to this position in life; it breaks down the trust between veterans and the charities who are there to support individuals.

"It damages the reputation of the service charities who are doing a lot to support individuals, and yet when you watch the AI videos, it would suggest that there's no support out there, and actually there is quite a lot of support out there."

Faye Tryhorne, from Alabaré, said: "As a general rule, veterans are well-regarded, and to be able to support them is a common cause.

"By having people scammed by buying these products, there's a risk that veterans who do need the support are left behind."

TikTok said it had removed all 45 accounts identified by the BBC, and in a statement said: "We enforce strict rules against harmfully misleading AI-generated content and scams, and we have removed the violative content and accounts shared with us.

"We continue to strengthen our safety strategies while also empowering our community with resources on how to navigate AI-generated content and how to spot and report potential scams."

A spokesperson for Meta, which owns Facebook and Instagram, said: "We don't allow content that uses deceptive or misleading practices and have removed the accounts and content that violate our policies.

"Our community standards apply to all content on our platforms regardless of whether it features AI-generated content or not."

A YouTube spokesperson said: "Upon review, we have terminated several of the flagged YouTube channels for violating our policies on spam, deceptive practices and scams."

articles.title: Daniel Thomas pleads not guilty after dinghy slashed in Channel
articles.summary: Daniel Thomas is accused of criminal damage after a video appeared to show him slashing at a dinghy.
articles.body:
Anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas has pleaded not guilty to criminal damage after a video appeared to show him slashing at a dinghy in the Channel with a knife.

The 37-year-old, known to his supporters as Danny Tommo, was arrested after the livestreamed video on Tuesday.

Thomas, who appeared at Basingstoke Magistrates' Court in Hampshire via videolink, is also charged with failing to disclose the PIN to his phone.

He pleaded not guilty to both charges and was remanded in custody until his next court appearance at Portsmouth Crown Court on 29 September.

The court heard a crew member was on the boat while it was heard leaking air.

Prosecutor Kevin Lucie, outlining the facts of the criminal damage charge, told the court that Thomas slashed an adrift boat with a knife and said: "You are on English territory. This is England. This is not France any more."

Deputy Chief Magistrate Tan Ikram said the case could have been heard in the magistrates' court but Mr Thomas elected to be tried at crown court.

Far-right activist Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, also known as Tommy Robinson, was among those in the public gallery.

Some supporters also gathered outside the court.

Posting on social media after the hearing, Yaxley-Lennon said: "Danny is being remanded to prison.

"His legal team will now prepare to fight at the crown court for his bail."

Hampshire police previously said an arrest had been made after a "boat that had an emergency responder on board" was damaged in the Channel on Tuesday.

Several hundred people gathered outside a police investigation centre in Basingstoke on Thursday evening, believing that Thomas was inside.

The demonstration, which seemed to pass off peacefully, began shortly before 18:30 BST. Protesters stood on the road outside the building and could be heard chanting "free DT".

The crowd began to disperse at about 21:45 after they learned of the charges against Thomas.

articles.title: 14 Kazakh military personnel killed during naval exercise, five naval officers detained over negligence suspicion
articles.summary: At least 14 Kazakh military personnel were killed after being swept away during a naval exercise on Thursday.
articles.body: At least 14 Kazakh military personnel were killed after being swept away during a naval exercise on Thursday. Following the incident, the authorities detained five defence officials on Friday.On Thursday, at least 17 servicemen were washed away in the Caspian Sea as they were disembarking from a patrol boat during a military exercise. Authorities reported that three were eventually rescued.The defence ministry said that it had concluded search and rescue efforts following the incident.“The leadership and personnel of the ministry of defense and the armed forces of the Republic of Kazakhstan extend their deepest and most sincere condolences to the families and loved ones of the deceased servicemen," the ministry said on Telegram.“The families of the fallen will receive all necessary comprehensive, financial, and psychological support,” it added.The exercise was reportedly being conducted during rough weather conditions over the sea.Anadolu Agency reported that the incident occurred “due to a sudden deterioration in weather conditions and intensifying winds,” and a commission led by defense minister Dauren Kosanov was immediately deployed to investigate the incident.According to the interior ministry, five military officials, including the first deputy navy commander, have been detained over allegations of negligence and navigation rule violations.Additionally, authorities reported that the decisions of detained military officials were being investigated, with the weather conditions and technical state of the boat being taken into accountKazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev declared Friday a nationwide day of mourning, expressing deep condolences.According to Reuters, Kazakhstan operates a small navy of about 3,000 personnel in the Caspian Sea and operates patrol and missile boats to protect its maritime border and offshore energy infrastructure.You use AI every day. articles.title: What’s in Iran’s seven-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz?
articles.summary: Tehran’s offer comes as high fuel prices put pressure on Trump ahead of the US midterm elections.
articles.body:
Iran says it has put forward a plan to the United States to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days, as Qatar passes messages between the two countries at the United Nations General Assembly in New York.

Speaking on the sidelines on Thursday, Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said the timetable could begin as soon as Washington accepted the proposal.

Both sides have described the indirect contact facilitated by Qatar in New York positively, but neither has indicated any diplomatic breakthrough as the war approaches its seven-month mark.

Analysts have told Al Jazeera a firm peace deal remains unlikely, with Iran still wanting to follow the approach set out in an earlier agreement, which would give it and Oman a main role in managing the strait before moving on to discussing terms for a broader peace deal.

For its part, the US, which has claimed to be “in total control” of the Strait of Hormuz, wants Iran’s nuclear programme to be the subject of discussions straight away.

Iran has previously made clear that it will not engage with broader peace talks, including addressing the issue of its nuclear programme, until the US naval blockade of its ports in and around the Hormuz strait is lifted, sanctions are repealed and the US provides a guarantee of an end to strikes, among other conditions.

Araghchi told reporters in New York that Iran had presented its plan to the US through intermediaries. “If certain conditions are met, the Strait of Hormuz would be open on the end of the seventh day and [peace] talks would restart,” he said.

He did not give details but said the proposal resembles the June 17 memorandum of understanding (MoU) signed by Iran and the US, which briefly eased the conflict before breaking down. “The moment they accept this plan, from the next day, this timetable can start, and after seven days, the strait will be open,” he said.

Under the June agreement, Iran undertook to allow ships to pass through the strait without paying tolls for 60 days – that was the period of time given for peace talks to take place. But the MoU left open what would happen after that period.

Al Jazeera’s Gabriel Elizondo reported while the new proposal is based on the MOU, “the Iranians are condensing the timeline and changing the sequence.”

“It would look something like this: fighting would stop on all fronts, including in Lebanon, the US would lift its naval blockade and oil sanctions, and release frozen Iranian assets. After seven days, the Strait of Hormuz would reopen. After that, talks on Iran’s nuclear programme would begin.”

However, Urban Coningham, a research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute, told Al Jazeera that Tehran is unlikely to receive any sanction relief. “Hormuz is a clear Iranian red line,” he told Al Jazeera. “The Iranians will not get reparations for the war, so control of the strait is the only way they can recover economically. I cannot see them backing down from that.”

The MoU signed in June set out an immediate halt to military operations on all fronts, including in Lebanon, where Israel has launched strikes and occupied part of the country, and triggered a 60-day period for negotiations on a lasting peace settlement. It included US waivers for Iranian oil exports and provisions to restore maritime traffic through the strait.

Similar to the Iranian proposal, it deferred other issues, including the future of Iran’s enriched uranium stockpile, to broader peace talks. But the agreement unravelled the following month amid renewed confrontation over shipping routes through the strait.

Coningham told Al Jazeera that Iran’s latest proposal follows this earlier model: “Open the strait within seven days, then start talks on the nuclear file.” But “the US does not want to compartmentalise the issues, it wants them discussed as one package”, he said.

How else does this new proposal place pressure on the US?

Coningham also sees a political calculation in making the offer publicly at the UN as Americans contend with high fuel prices. “By explicitly saying this may be the only chance before the midterms, Iran is putting pressure on Trump over oil and gas prices and the strait,” he said. “It is a tactic to put more pressure on the US.”

The strait, which runs between Iran and Oman, is a vital route for oil and gas exports from the Gulf. Disruption to shipping has driven up energy prices far beyond the region, giving both governments an economic reason to reach an agreement despite their differences.

With the US midterm elections approaching, a deal to get it reopened could give Trump a chance to bring down fuel prices before voters go to the polls – potentially giving the Republican Party a much-needed electoral boost before the midterms.

Trump has presented the electoral calculation differently, however. In his address to the General Assembly on Tuesday, he accused Iran of waiting to see how his Republican Party performs in November and predicted a deal would happen after the vote. He also threatened to “annihilate the Islamic Republic” if there was no agreement.

Trump claimed the election did not affect his own decision-making on Iran: “The only thing that does is that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon.”

That leaves an open question about whether the prospect of lower energy prices is enough to persuade his administration to accept Iran’s proposed order of talks. Coningham doubts it. “Trump is prepared for this to go on through the midterms,” he said. “The same problem remains where the proposal does not answer questions about the nuclear file.”

Where do broader US-Iran peace talks stand?

Araghchi met US envoy Steve Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner on Tuesday in talks mediated by Qatar. The Iranian foreign minister described the exchange as productive and said messages continued to pass between the sides.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said it would be wrong to describe the meeting as a major breakthrough, however.

Burcu Ozcelik, a senior research fellow for Middle East security, told Al Jazeera that the major blockage for Washington and Tehran is that each is making different assumptions about how much pressure they can exert on the other. The Trump administration is unlikely to revive the failed MoU, she said, because it assesses its naval blockade and tighter sanctions as working.

“The US appears to believe it can wait this out until Tehran is prepared to make meaningful concessions,” Ozcelik said.

“But Iran remains defiant despite indications that it is hurting economically.”

articles.title: Putin’s party secures a record number of seats in Russia’s wartime election
articles.summary: Russian authorities on Friday released the full results from the country’s first wartime parliamentary election, which further cemented the Kremlin’s overwhelming political control.
articles.body: Russian authorities on Friday released the full results from the country’s first wartime parliamentary election, which further cemented the Kremlin’s overwhelming political control. The three-day balloting ended Sunday. According to the results released by the Central Election Commission, the main Kremlin party, United Russia, will get more than three-fourths of the seats in the lower house, the State Duma, a record high. The tightly orchestrated vote excluded virtually any genuine opposition. Nearly 60% of the 111 million eligible voters turned out, the most for a parliamentary election in over a decade. Authorities had spread the voting over three days and allowed online voting in some regions to boost participation. The parliamentary election was the first since President Vladimir Putin launched the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and the first to include residents of four regions of that country that were seized and illegally annexed by Moscow later that year. Voting also was held in Crimea, which was illegally annexed by Russia in 2014. Kyiv denounced the voting in those regions as illegal. Putin declared Wednesday that the election results was a show of public support for the Kremlin policies. A massive state media campaign and tight control over the election allowed the Kremlin to strengthen its political dominance despite economic troubles and long-range Ukrainian drone attacks. Central Election Commission chief Ella Pamfilova said that United Russia got 349 out of 450 Duma seats. It polled just under 58% of the ballot for the 225 seats apportioned by parties and also won 209 single-seat races that fill the other half of the chamber. Several smaller parties representing the “systemic opposition” that vote in line with the Kremlin wishes on all key issues won 97 seats, and the remaining four seats were filled by candidates who ran without a party affiliation, Pamfilova said. United Russia and other parties said they put dozens of Ukraine war veterans on its lists. The liberal Yabloko party, the only registered political entity that dared to publicly criticize the war, was removed from the ballot last month by Russia’s Supreme Court. It only had a few dozen candidates in the single-seat races and none of them won a seat. The election took place against the backdrop of incessant Ukrainian drone attacks. On Sunday, Russia’s Defense Ministry reported it downed 1,110 drones overnight. Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 450 drones were downed while flying toward the city on Sunday in what he described as “the largest ever” attack on the capital in a failed attempt to disrupt the vote. The attack, which damaged an oil refinery and a residential building, killed three people and injured 38 in the wider Moscow region, officials said. Pamfilova said six polling workers were killed in Ukrainian attacks and 75 polling stations were damaged or destroyed by shelling during the voting.

articles.title: Pakistan, Turkiye edge closer towards joining Saudi war against Houthis
articles.summary: Pakistani and Turkish military chiefs head to Riyadh for urgent talks, but both countries remain cautious on involvement
articles.body:
Islamabad, Pakistan — Turkiye and Pakistan are rushing their military chiefs to Riyadh in response to a call from Saudi Arabia for an urgent meeting on implementing their mutual defence agreement, amid the escalating war against the Houthis in Yemen that has spilled over into Saudi territory.

Turkiye’s Defence Ministry confirmed on Friday that General Selcuk Bayraktaroglu, the chief of general staff, will be travelling to Saudi Arabia.

Pakistan’s chief of defence forces, Field Marshal Asim Munir , is also expected to arrive in the Saudi capital soon, Al Jazeera has learned, though the Inter-Services Public Relations , Pakistan’s military media wing, did not respond to a request for confirmation on whether Munir had departed for Riyadh.

The developments follow a Saudi request to Turkiye and Pakistan for their military chiefs to convene, following weeks of Houthi missile and drone attacks on Saudi territory.

The Houthis said on Thursday they had fired dozens of missiles and drones at Saudi targets, including a claimed strike on a “sensitive target” in Riyadh and on Saudi Aramco facilities in Yanbu. Saudi authorities said air defences intercepted six ballistic missiles aimed at Taif and Yanbu, and issued emergency alerts for Mecca, Jeddah and Yanbu.

The Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, signed on August 7, treats an attack on any one of Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan as an attack on all three.

Saudi Arabia’s account of the days before Friday’s meeting showed how urgently Riyadh sees the crisis.

The meeting between three chiefs of staff was first announced after a meeting in New York on September 24 between the Saudi Foreign Minister, Prince Faisal bin Farhan, Pakistan’s Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister, Ishaq Dar, and Turkish Foreign Minister, Hakan Fidan.

According to the Saudi foreign ministry, they discussed arrangements for an urgent chiefs of staff meeting to explore ways of supporting Saudi Arabia under the pact.

The statement condemned attacks targeting Mecca and civilian and economic facilities in the kingdom, and affirmed Saudi Arabia’s right to defend itself under Article 51 of the UN Charter.

Pakistan’s account of the same meeting sounded more cautious.

“Under the framework of the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement (MJDA), we reviewed progress towards establishing the institutional structures under the agreement and exchanged views on regional and international security issues,” Dar posted on X.

Turkiye’s foreign ministry struck a similarly measured tone at the New York meeting. Turkish state media described it as a review of ongoing “technical negotiations” towards institutionalising the pact, ahead of a future meeting of its Strategic Political and Defence Committee .

Days earlier, Fidan had struck a notably different note in a live interview with Turkish broadcaster NTV.

“Our agreement includes an alliance commitment, we stand by our word,” he said. “Their military needs could particularly be in certain technical areas and we wouldn’t have any problem meeting that.”

Neither Islamabad’s nor Ankara’s account of the New York meeting mentioned the Houthi attacks that had prompted the Saudi statement.

That caution may be connected to direct warnings the Houthis have issued to both countries, say analysts.

The Iran-backed Houthis have in recent days made dramatic territorial gains against Yemen’s Saudi-backed, internationally recognised government forces. They seized the strategic port city of Mocha and then almost the entire Red Sea coast, including several islands. That has given the group greater control over the Bab al-Mandeb strait, the critically important maritime passage that Saudi Arabia was using to ship oil out after the US-Iran war effectively shut down the Strait of Hormuz. This week, the Houthis also made advances towards Yemen’s highlands, even as battles with Saudi-backed government forces have escalated.

They have launched missiles and drones at Saudi Arabia — and threatened allies.

Mohammed al-Bukhaiti, a member of the Houthi movement’s political bureau, told an Iraqi television programme this week that Pakistan and Turkiye would be met with an “iron fist” if they entered the war.

Tughral Yamin, a retired brigadier and senior associate at Islamabad’s Institute of Policy Studies, told Al Jazeera the constraints run on both sides of the pact.

“Sending troops would be difficult because the Pakistan Army is stretched thin on ground due to external and internal threats,” he said, referring to ongoing border clashes with Afghanistan, persistent tensions with India and mounting attacks domestically by armed groups. “It is also subject to speculation if Turkiye would be willing to divert troops to Saudi Arabia. Turkiye has its commitments to NATO and its border with Syria is not entirely secure.”

The Saudi religious establishment has struck an even more urgent note than the foreign ministry.

Grand Mufti Sheikh Saleh Al-Fawzan called on forces to “stand united against this misguided sect and deviant group”, referring to the Houthis.

He described defending the kingdom’s borders as a duty “for which lives and souls are sacrificed”.

In a rare message, Saudi King Salman struck a similar note days earlier, accusing the Houthis of attempting to strike Mecca again and telling a cabinet meeting in Jeddah that the attempt violated Islam’s holiest sites.

Gokhan Ereli, an international relations expert at Istanbul’s Ibn Haldun University, told Al Jazeera that the mufti’s message was significant domestically, even if its practical effect on Pakistan and Turkiye is limited.

“The mufti’s authority actually carries real weight in Saudi Arabia domestically, and this statement works above all as a mobilisation tool aimed at soldiers on the front line, giving a long, costly war a spiritual, religious anchor that makes sacrifices easier to accept,” he said.

“For Pakistan and Turkiye, the effect is more about tone than the obligation. Both governments already engage with Riyadh through existing security arrangements, and religious framing mainly reinforces the language of solidarity without altering the formal terms of those commitments,” the academic added.

A regional diplomat told Al Jazeera the messaging reflects a broader shift.

“The [Saudi] public have become increasingly aware of the threat of the Houthis, regularly receiving sirens warning of Houthi missile strikes usually aimed at civilian infrastructure,” the diplomat said, speaking on condition of anonymity. “But this speech signifies a broader approach to raising civilian awareness and a reflection that things are likely to get worse, not better.”

Turkish Parliament Speaker Numan Kurtulmus said on Friday that the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement had not yet been submitted for parliamentary approval. He expected it to be formally submitted when the assembly returns from recess on October 1.

Under Turkiye’s constitution, international agreements only take effect once parliament ratifies them.

Two days before the New York meeting, Pakistan’s Foreign Office announced that retired Lieutenant General Nauman Mahmood had been appointed as the pact’s first secretary general.

Mahmood is a former senior officer at the Inter-Services Intelligence, Pakistan’s main spy agency, and will lead the pact’s General Secretariat being set up in Riyadh.

“In practical terms, Pakistan has just sent a retired three-star general to Riyadh to assume the office of the secretary general of the Joint Defence Alliance,” Yamin said. “The task before him would be to assess the situation quickly and come up with some realistic answers.”

Pakistan “already has advisers, trainers, logisticians and technicians on the ground [in Saudi Arabia] under past bilateral protocols,” he added.

In April, Riyadh confirmed the arrival of a Pakistani military force, including fighter and support aircraft, at King Abdulaziz airbase in the kingdom’s Eastern province. That deployment under the two countries’ Strategic Mutual Defence Agreement, signed last September, came amid attacks on Saudi Arabia from Iran.

Pakistan has trained thousands of Saudi military personnel since 1967 and stationed troops in the kingdom since the 1970s, including to protect oil infrastructure in the Eastern Province.

Ereli said Saudi Arabia’s difficulty was not a lack of resources.

“Saudi Arabia’s resources, airpower and the years of external backing are there,” he said. “The real difficulty here lies in a fragmented, multi-actor coalition on the ground [in Yemen]. Limited US military commitment has left Riyadh carrying most of the operational weight on its own, straining its air defence capacity.”

France and Britain have offered defensive support. Britain agreed this week to refuel Saudi jets on defensive missions. France confirmed on Friday that it is sending troops to guard the major oil terminal at Yanbu, the Red Sea port that Saudi Arabia has been using to bypass the Strait of Hormuz.

Despite the mounting show of support from Pakistan, Turkiye, France and Britain, the regional diplomat said the Houthis show no sign of easing off in their campaign against Saudi Arabia and the forces it backs in Yemen.

“The Houthis have demonstrated their willingness and ability to target both civilian and military targets in Saudi Arabia and intend to continue to do so,” the diplomat said. “It’s clear Saudi Arabia is preparing for a sustained increase in tempo of operations which may include further loss of life.”

“Fighting is more contested than most think,” the diplomat added. “[Saudi-backed] coalition forces suffered a major logistical and operational setback in Mocha but are progressing slowly on the remaining fronts, and a battle may have been lost, but the war is yet to be decided.”

Yamin, for his part, said he was hopeful cooler heads would prevail.

“I hope a diplomatic solution would resolve the conflict, because none of us would like our country to get entangled in a war that is not of our making,” he said.

articles.title: Humanitarian crisis worsens in Ceuta as thousands remain stranded
articles.summary: People face harsh conditions, overcrowding, limited aid, and alleged abuse while awaiting decisions on their future.
articles.body:
Ceuta, Spain – For more than a month, 21-year-old Anis Fadi, a university graduate and qualified accountant, has been sleeping in a makeshift shelter.

At the end of July, he crossed the border from Morocco to the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, on the North African coast, along with about 70,000 others.

At his migrant camp on Trampolin Beach, he queues for hours each day for food at a Red Cross centre.

“I don’t even have a tent,” he told Al Jazeera. “We make shelter with old pieces of wood, sticks from broken branches, and whatever else we find here.”

When the wind blows, these makeshift shelters offer little protection, and soon the temperature will dip.

“There are a lot of people worse than me,” said Fadi.

The Spanish government estimates that between 6,000 and 10,000 who made the crossing remain stranded. Officials in Ceuta believe the figure is closer to 13,000 people.

About 5,000 – mostly women and children – have been given temporary accommodation by the authorities. The rest sleep outside.

Fadi said, as he waits for food in the heat, police officers with batons shout orders at the crowds.

“It’s a hard life here,” he said, but he does not regret leaving Morocco.

“Life was harder there for me. I didn’t see any future for myself.”

More than 100 people died in the crossing. Fadi said he swam for hours to reach Ceuta, believing it was a gateway to Europe, where he imagines a better life awaits.

He believes men like him who “have the skills … don’t have the chance”.

“We are not criminals,” he said, in response to the anti-migration rhetoric and protests that followed the crossing. “We just want to work.”

Right-wing European politicians have framed the Ceuta crossing as a threatening invasion.

In Spain, protests have erupted against the government’s handling of the crisis.

Ceuta is usually home to about 84,000 people. Its population almost doubled at the outset of this crisis. Though most have returned, the enclave has been struggling to cope with the pressure of hosting those who remain.

After a new temporary shelter opened up recently, offering space for about 1,700 people, it hit capacity within hours.

As humanitarian groups struggle to provide basic needs, Nolte Bauer, from Mission Lifeline International, said migrants also feel unsafe.

“Outside the official camps there is a lack of basic hygiene,” he said. “There is insufficient medical aid and the immediate danger of violence, especially at night.”

His organisation often receives reports of people being beaten.

Several people interviewed by Al Jazeera said they had been abused by men in military or police uniforms. Some were wounded, with cuts to the head or bruising around the body.

“These are racist people, these soldiers,” one man who requested anonymity told Al Jazeera. “They found me sleeping and they started to hit me without any reason. They broke one of my hands; they wanted to break the other one. They also beat me on my knees.”

Some said they were afraid to go to hospital, fearing they could be deported, and instead sought help from aid groups. NGO volunteers told Al Jazeera they had treated wounded men.

But Spanish authorities rejected any claims of abuse and discrimination, telling Al Jazeera that the police acts “with absolute respect for human rights”.

They say they are expanding accommodation and providing food and medical care while migrants are identified and their cases are processed.

The government has said the aim is to return to Morocco those who do not have a legal status to remain in Spain, while Ceuta’s leaders have repeatedly called on Madrid and Europe for more support.

articles.title: Man searching with metal detector unearths massive Viking Age fortune, shattering records
articles.summary: A metal detectorist in Finland uncovered an enormous Viking Age silver hoard of over 4,000 coins near Sysmä, more than doubling the country's previous record find.
articles.body: A metal detectorist in Finland unearthed a massive Viking Age silver hoard estimated to contain more than 4,000 coins — the largest discovery of its kind ever found in the country. The hoard, uncovered by metal detectorist Kalle Lappinen, was found near the village center of Sysmä, a town about 105 miles northeast of Helsinki. Lappinen discovered the hoard on Sept. 3 and promptly reported it to authorities. Archaeologists from Lahti Museums began recovering the silver the very next day. PUZZLING SOUND IN BACKYARD LEADS HOMEOWNER TO MASSIVE 1,000-YEAR-OLD TREASURE The hoard consists of "thousands of silver coins, hack silver, a silver bracelet, a mount and a bead," according to a museum release. The hoard includes coins from present-day Sweden, Britain and Germany, as well as dirhams originating from areas that are now part of Turkey and Iran. The recovered coins weigh approximately 10 pounds in total and are believed to date to between 1000 and 1050 A.D., as Lahti Museums archaeologist Esko Tikkala told Fox News Digital. Tikkala oversaw the hoard's recovery. He said the dating remains preliminary and will be refined after the coins have been cleaned and thoroughly studied. MYSTERIOUS 3,000-YEAR-OLD HOARD WITH VIOLENTLY SMASHED SWORD EMERGES DURING CONSTRUCTION PROJECT While Tikkala has excavated other Late Iron Age hoards in the region, he said the sheer size of the Sysmä discovery surprised him. "Instead of the tens or few hundreds of coins we usually encounter, this find contains thousands," he said. Even at this preliminary stage, Tikkala said the discovery adds to evidence that Sysmä was an important hub during the Late Iron Age, with trade connections extending in multiple directions. "Today, Sysmä might be regarded as a relatively modest and peripheral place, but judging from the Late Iron Age archaeological material, the situation seems to have been very different a thousand years ago," he said. ANCIENT VIKING SWORD DISCOVERED 'STICKING UP OUT OF THE GROUND' AFTER 1,300 YEARS The hoard also contains more than twice as many coins as Finland's previously largest known Viking Age coin hoard, which was unearthed in Nousiainen in 1895 and contained approximately 1,700 coins, Tikkala added. The identity of the hoard's owner has been lost to time, Tikkala said, though several theories exist about why the silver was buried. "It is very difficult to determine what actually happened or who the owner was." The coins and other objects were buried beside a low rocky outcrop in spots where they could have been relatively easily recovered, he added. Why their owner never returned for the treasure, however, remains a mystery. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER "Perhaps a merchant buried part of his wealth for safekeeping so that he did not have to carry it with him, intending to retrieve it the next time he returned to the area," Tikkala said. "Alternatively, it may have belonged to a wealthy local inhabitant who buried it because of the threat of conflict or an enemy attack," he added. "There are many possible explanations, and it is very difficult to determine what actually happened or who the owner was." Frida Ehrnsten, keeper of the numismatic collections at the National Museum of Finland, told Fox News Digital that the discovery could give researchers a new understanding of how silver circulated in the region roughly 1,000 years ago. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS "It’s a very, very, very important new find that will in some ways probably change our perception of the Viking Age silver economy here," Ehrnsten said. Ehrnsten noted that researchers generally do not describe the people living in Finland during the period as Vikings — as Vikings came from Scandinavia, which does not include Finland — though the term "Viking Age" is used to describe the broader era and cultural context. She said one of the most intriguing aspects of the discovery is that the silver was found in two separate deposits roughly 39 feet apart. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "It’s kind of a double hoard," she said. "We haven’t really had any known examples of those from before." Ehrnsten also noted that hobby metal detectorists have played a major role in the surge of archaeological coin discoveries across Finland. About 25 years ago, roughly 7,000 Viking Age coins were known from Finland, she said. Today, that number stands at around 14,000. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Almost the whole body of this new material is made by people who go around searching [as] a hobby," she added.

articles.title: Zuckerberg softens his look with some geeky tweaks — and a message
articles.summary: Clothes can often tell a story. In Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg’s case, he’s really spelling it out for us.
articles.body: Clothes can often tell a story. In Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg’s case, he’s really spelling it out for us. Appearing Wednesday at a company event in Menlo Park, California, Zuckerberg opted for a shirt that carried an overt message — and an apt one at that, considering he was showcasing the latest Meta designs in AI and wearable tech. Zuckerberg’s oversized black T-shirt bore the words “BUILDING IS MY LOVE LANGUAGE,” in Serif font. The boxy shirt looked similar to others Zuck has previously had custom-made via a partnership with Los Angeles-based designer Mike Amiri. Reps for Meta and Amiri didn’t respond to requests for comment on his latest piece, but it was yet another reminder that Zuckerberg’s days of traditional tech-bro hoodies and tight, heather-grey T-shirts are long behind him. Still, he appeared to make some subtle tweaks to the more swaggering streetwear-inspired look he has been sporting in recent years. For one, his mustard brown trousers with a notably preppy pleat down their front. But more prominently, Zuckerberg wore a few different pairs of Meta’s AI-augmented, Ray-Ban eyeglasses. One had a thicker frame in tortoise shell, but the glasses he wore when he first stepped on stage were a more traditional Browline pair with a bold upper frame — a style first introduced by Shuron in 1947 that became a staple of 1950s style. This new Meta pair of “audio glasses” in Ray-Ban’s Clubmaster style feature microphones and AI connect ability but no camera, in concession to privacy advocates. “Style is important,” Zuckerberg told the crowd in his keynote address, “because if you’re going to be wearing glasses all day long, they have to be great glasses first. Before we even talk about any technology, the design needs to be glasses that you want to wear.” A message about love and the geeky slant to the Facebook founder’s on-stage look arguably softens the Manosphere-like image he has adopted, with gold chain jewelry and baggy silhouettes. And he’d be wise to do this if he wants to prove that he can be trusted with what may be the most rapidly advancing – and many fear dangerous – technology in the world. Verge senior correspondent Tom Warren likened Wednesday’s new look to the 🤓 nerd emoji in a sign Zuckerberg had perhaps achieved his goal. Derek Guy, the menswear writer behind the @dieworkwear accounts, noted the tech mogul’s new glasses were most strongly associated with establishment figures or intellectuals from the ‘50s and ‘60s. “It gives off an air of intellectualism, government-man seriousness,” Guy said. Guy also noted how far Zuckerberg had come since being the “whiz-kid hacker… poster child of not caring about style,” but said he suspected this was just a sign of his age, rather than anything outwardly political, as some have speculated. “Mark Zuckerberg still is basically a T-shirt and pants — and sometimes hoodies — guy, but the choices are much more intentional,” Guy said. “It’s a little bit more directional … a little bit more stylish.” Zuckerberg’s image is likely to take another hit next month when Aaron Sorkin’s movie “The Social Reckoning” hits theaters. In that movie, a sequel to 2010’s “The Social Network,” Zuckerberg is played by “Succession” star Jeremy Strong, as he navigates the fallout from the 2021 leak about the company’s handling of misinformation and other sensitive issues. In the film’s trailer, Strong sports the same unfortunate Caesar haircut the tech founder had in the late 2010s and early 2020s — something Zuckerberg has replaced in recent years by growing out his natural curls. Zuckerberg wasn’t the only one drawing attention for his sartorial choices at Wednesday’s event. Alexandr Wang, Meta’s chief AI officer, appeared on stage wearing a loose, green camo T-shirt emblazoned with drawings of White-tailed deer and the words “Lake Tahoe” that he said he’d thrifted in Santa Cruz, California, for $30. He finished his look with a slightly tapered pair of “falketind” hiking pants from Norwegian outfitter Norrøna (featuring one comically large pocket), a pair of Crocs from the Realtree Camo Collection, and a boxy pair of eyeglasses with a thin wire frame. Perhaps thanks to Wang’s messy mullet, the whole look had something of a gas station chic vibe. “Dress for the job you want,” Wang wrote on X.

articles.title: US seeking to revive Russia-Ukraine ceasefire talks
articles.summary: Ukraine’s president added that eight regions have come under attack by Russian forces since the start of the day.
articles.body:
The United States is working to arrange a new round of talks in a bid to end the four-and-a-half-year Russia-Ukraine war .

Kyiv and Moscow both confirmed the plan to relaunch trilateral talks on Friday. The move follows negotiations that started earlier this year before the US efforts to broker an end to hostilities petered out amid Washington’s war on Iran.

The United Arab Emirates is mooted as the host of the new talks.

“The American side has proposed meeting at a technical level in a three-way ⁠⁠format,” Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told reporters. “We are awaiting a ⁠⁠proposal from the United States ⁠⁠regarding the date ⁠⁠and the US has suggested the Emirates as ‌‌a possible location.”

Later, the Kremlin confirmed that a trilateral meeting could be soon, although spokesman Dmitry Peskov said there were no details to ⁠⁠add currently.

President Donald Trump’s envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Russia and Ukraine earlier this month in a bid to jump-start the bid to secure a ceasefire.

The US stance has previously been criticised for favouring Russia’s narrative, with Moscow insisting that Ukraine cede territory that Russia has illegally occupied, demilitarise and drop ambitions to join NATO.

Russia’s presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev reportedly met with Witkoff ‌‌and ‌‌Kushner in the US on September 24. Peskov said those talks were about potential economic cooperation.

Zelenskyy said that Trump told him that Ukraine will be granted permission to produce advanced Patriot air defence missiles.

Kyiv desperately needs additional air defences to counter Russia’s increasing drone and missile attacks, but Trump has delayed approval.

Should a licence be issued, it would be more than a year before Kyiv could put any new Patriot systems into service, leaving Zelenskyy, in the US to attend the United Nations General Assembly, to continue his pleas for additional support from allies.

“In recent days, during our meetings, Ukraine has openly informed our partners: Russia will only escalate as winter approaches unless there is pressure,” Zelenskyy wrote on X on Friday. “For diplomacy to work, US sanctions must be implemented and European sanctions must be strengthened.”

Kyiv is also talking with European Union representatives about the need to accelerate budget support for the military, warning that Ukraine risks running out of missiles and drones early next year.

Both Moscow and Kyiv continue to launch nightly barrages against one another.

Overnight attacks struck a 16-floor building in Kyiv’s central Pechersk district, killing a 14-year-old boy and injuring at least seven other people.

In the southern Odesa region, Governor Oleh Kiper said one person was killed ‌‌and another injured in a series of “massive” Russian strikes on a residential area and logistics premises ‌‌of a ‌‌postal operator.

Russia said its air defence ⁠⁠units destroyed about ⁠⁠50 drones over the Rostov region overnight and a drone attack damaged ⁠⁠the Novoshakhtinsk oil refinery, forcing it to suspend operations.

Ukraine recently struck two other major ‌‌Russian ‌‌oil refineries in Moscow and Yaroslavl. Zelenskyy asserted that refineries ⁠⁠in Bashkortostan and ⁠⁠the Samara ⁠⁠region had also been hit in the past 24-hours.

The Ukrainian leader also reported unspecified strikes in the Black Sea. He added that he has held talks with India, Turkiye, ⁠⁠Egypt and other Middle Eastern countries concerning efforts to unblock shipping in the Black Sea, where Russia has targeted cargo vessels.

articles.title: Fighting in northern Ethiopia spurs fears of blackout and blockade
articles.summary: Tigray was cut off from the world during the 2020-2022 civil war, which killed around 600,000 people.
articles.body:
Fears of a communications blackout in northern Ethiopia have increased as fighting flares between the federal military and forces from the Tigray region and ⁠their allies.

Telecom and internet networks were reported to have stopped working on Friday as the conflict threatened to develop across the country into a full-scale war .

The interruptions have provoked fears of a repeat of the communications blackout and supplies blockade during the 2020-2022 civil war in ⁠northern Ethiopia, when Tigray was largely cut off from the outside world.

Web monitor NetBlocks said it had detected an “internet disruption in northern Ethiopia corresponding to reports of a telecoms blackout in Tigray”.

The Reuters news agency reported that Tigray’s ruling party, the Tigray People’s Liberation Front, had ordered private operator Safaricom and state-owned Ethio telecom to cut off access ⁠to phone and internet networks in the region.

A source said the restrictions may be part of a tactic to neutralise the advantage of government forces using battlefield drones.

Lower-level clashes between federal and Tigrayan forces have been ongoing for some time. However, fighting intensified this week across Tigray and later spread to the neighbouring Afar and Amhara regions, after seven armed groups announced they have formed an alliance .

The Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival has committed itself to removing the government of Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed.

The Tigray Army said the federal government had launched a “full-scale offensive” involving infantry, mechanised units and drones, and said its forces had begun what they called a defensive war to counter aggression by Abiy’s government.

The alliance forces have seized three airports and launched attacks against ⁠federal troops in Afar and Amhara.

The ⁠federal government has accused Eritrea of financially backing the TPLF and its allies, which leaders in the capital Asmara deny.

Abdisalam Balema, a member of the Tigray People’s Liberation Front’s (TPLF) central committee, told Al Jazeera that the situation has become a “full war”.

The outbreak of violence is the most serious escalation ⁠since the civil war in 2020-2022. During that conflict, which killed an estimated 600,000 people, the telecoms blackout and supplies blockade imposed on Tigray caused famine-like conditions for hundreds of thousands of people.

People in Tigray are reported to have rushed to stock up on basic supplies and withdraw cash.

The renewed fighting comes at an awkward moment for the United States, which only this month lifted sanctions on Ethiopia and Eritrea related to atrocities committed during the last civil war, saying the “national emergency… has expired”.

The conflict could also draw in neighbouring Eritrea, which fears landlocked Ethiopia is planning to invade it to gain access to the Red Sea.

articles.title: Microsoft opens Hyd cloud region, boosts T’s bid to host 5GW data centre capacity by 2029
articles.summary: Microsoft opens India South Central cloud region near Hyderabad, its largest in India, supporting AI demand and boosting Telangana’s 5GW data centre target by 2029.
articles.body: Hyderabad: Microsoft opened its largest hyperscale region in India, the India South Central cloud region, at Chandanvelly on the outskirts of Hyderabad on Thursday. Its second data centre in Hyderabad, the facility is part of Microsoft’s larger investment of $20.5 billion in AI infrastructure in India by 2030.The new cloud region, Microsoft’s fourth in India after existing ones in Chennai, Hyderabad and Pune, has a resilient three-zone architecture and is roughly equivalent to two Eden Gardens stadiums combined in size, Microsoft said. The region is designed to support demand for cloud, AI and high-density compute services across India and the wider region.Inaugurating the facility, Telangana IT and industries minister D Sridhar Babu said the investment adds momentum to Telangana’s aspirations of achieving 5 GW of data centre capacity by 2029 as part of its strategic AI roadmap and of targeting around $30 billion in investment across the broader AI and digital infrastructure ecosystem by then.“Microsoft’s investment will further strengthen Hyderabad’s ability to power the next generation of AI, cloud and digital innovation for India and the world. It is aligned with Telangana’s Hyderabad Global AI Strategy, which brings together AI City, the Global AI Innovation Hub, AIKAM and TGDeX to support the development and adoption of AI at scale,” Sridhar Babu said.Telangana currently has 300 MW of data centre capacity already operational and 2 GW under development across global and Indian operators. Microsoft, AWS, Iron Mountain, CtrlS, Sify, TCL, NTT DATA and CapitaLand are among companies investing in the state, with the new projects increasingly being designed for AI-scale compute, high-density GPUs, hyperscale cloud and advanced cooling.Microsoft India and South Asia president Puneet Chandok said Hyderabad’s talent base, innovation ecosystem and AI-ready cloud infrastructure position the city to power AI transformation for customers across the region.Rajiv Kumar, managing director and president of Microsoft India Development Centre, said the company would continue to support local communities through skilling, workforce development and sustainability initiatives.Microsoft said the Hyderabad data centre region operates with effectively zero water use for cooling and is backed by groundwater recharge, rainwater harvesting and watershed resilience programmes. articles.title: Iraq's Najaf airport halts Iran flights as Tehran threatens countries with airspace disruption
articles.summary: Iraq's Najaf International Airport halted all flights to and from Iran on Friday, effective until further notice.
articles.body: Iraq's Najaf International Airport halted all flights to and from Iran on Friday, effective until further notice.In a statement released through Iraq's state news agency (INA), the airport's administration said that, per official directives from the competent authorities, all flights to and from the Islamic Republic of Iran would be suspended beginning from 2am Friday, (2300 GMT Thursday), with no set date for resumption.The airport called on all relevant parties to take appropriate action and inform airlines and other operators accordingly, noting that any decision to restart flights would be communicated through an official announcement.Following the announcement, Advisor to the Iranian leader, Mohammad Mokhber, threatened regional countries with airspace disruption.He said if Iran could not have flights and receive airport service, “no one in the region can either”, Reuters reported, citing Nournews.On Tuesday, Iran's civil aviation organisation announced that flights between Tehran and both Baghdad and Oman's Muscat would be halted starting early Wednesday.Later, the United Arab Emirates announced suspending flights operated by Iranian airlines to and from the country, joining Oman, Iraq, Azerbaijan, Georgia and Turkmenistan.The announcement comes after US treasury secretary Scott Bessent said on Tuesday that Iranian airlines' operations worldwide would cease as of Wednesday, as part of sanctions targeting Iran.With the US-Israeli war against Iran having reached a prolonged stalemate for months, Washington has signalled a change in strategy. The new financial sanctions will target firms in countries that conduct business with Iranian companies, an approach commonly referred to as "secondary sanctions."The country has also warned that airports and companies continuing to service sanctioned Iranian carriers could risk losing access to the US dollar financial system.You use AI every day. articles.title: A Kentucky woman spent 35 years turning 45 acres into a nature preserve; now a nearly $40 million sewer project has secured seven easements across her land through eminent domain, triggering fresh county scrutiny
articles.summary: A Kentucky woman who spent 35 years turning her 45-acre property into a natural area is facing a major change to the land after a nearly $40 million sewer
articles.body: A Kentucky woman who spent 35 years turning her 45-acre property into a natural area is facing a major change to the land after a nearly $40 million sewer project secured easements across it. The Central Boone County Sewer project, being built by Sanitation District 1 (SD1), will use part of Gayle Pille’s property for a new sewer pipeline.Pille has spent decades developing the property into a nature preserve. According to WVXU, she planted native shrubs and trees, cleaned up creek crossings and built bird houses. She also plans to donate the land to the Boone Conservancy after her death so it can remain a community nature preserve.The sewer project has four phases and is designed to increase wastewater capacity in central Boone County. Its final phase includes about 3.2 miles of new sewer line, known as B.2. The route has become the subject of protests from Pille’s neighbours and supporters, who want SD1 to consider moving the line away from her property.The issue has now drawn the attention of Boone County officials. Boone County Judge/Executive Gary Moore sent a letter to SD1 asking the agency to explain why it selected the current route. Commissioner Chet Hand has also asked SD1 Executive Director Adam Chaney to present a report to the county fiscal court explaining the criteria used to select the route.Why the sewer line crosses Pille’s landSD1 is building the Central Boone County Sewer project to redirect wastewater currently going to the Dry Creek Wastewater Treatment Plant in Villa Hills westward to the Western Regional Water Reclamation Facility in Petersburg.One part of the project requires the agency to use eminent domain to obtain access to Pille’s property. Eminent domain is the government’s authority to acquire private property for public use without the owner’s consent.SD1 and Pille were unable to reach an agreement on a buyout for the land. The agency then took the matter to the Boone County Circuit Court. According to the reports, the court ruled in favour of SD1, allowing the agency to acquire the property needed for the sewer project.SD1 secured seven easements on parts of Pille’s property. The Boone County Circuit Court decision has been appealed by Pille, and the case remains pending.Construction has not yet started on the part involving her property. Attorney Jon Woodall told WVXU that there is currently nothing legally stopping the project from moving forward, although the dispute over compensation can continue.“You're just dealing with compensation, that's it. And the project can go forward while you're fighting about the dollars, Woodall said."Pille’s 35-year effort to preserve the landThe dispute is not only about the sewer line. Pille has spent decades changing the property into a natural area and hopes it will remain protected after her death.She spent 35 years developing the property by planting native shrubs and trees, cleaning up creek crossings and putting up bird houses. Her plan was to eventually leave the land to the Boone Conservancy.The property, however, did not have a conservation easement at the time of the dispute. Pille had hoped to place one on the land in the future.SD1 initially offered Pille $22,100 for her 45 acres. A survey conducted by SD1 later found that the trees Pille had planted were worth about $1.5 million.The disagreement over the property has also led to public protests. Pille’s neighbours and other supporters have opposed the B.2 route and have held protests outside SD1’s headquarters in Fort Wright.They have also spoken at Boone County Fiscal Court meetings, asking county officials to put pressure on SD1 to consider another route.County asks SD1 to explain routeJennifer Watts, one of Pille’s neighbours, has been involved in the campaign against the B.2 route. She told SD1 board members that several possible routes had been considered before the current one was selected.“I know they had multiple routes to choose from, and they chose the one that goes through — it requires them to go through 18 properties,” Watts said.At a Boone County Fiscal Court meeting on Tuesday, Watts asked county officials to play a role in the dispute, while acknowledging that the court could not decide Pille’s eminent domain case.“We understand that this court cannot decide Gayle Pille’s eminent domain case, and we are not asking you to take over SD1’s engineering decisions, but there is a difference between not controlling SD1 and having no role at all,” Watts said.Moore said he understood the concerns but believed it would be irresponsible for the fiscal court to try to influence SD1’s engineering decision. He said the utility had more information about the project and was better positioned to decide the appropriate route.Moore said his request for information was meant to advocate for residents rather than interfere with SD1’s engineering decisions.Kentucky changes eminent domain rulesThe dispute has also brought attention to recent changes to Kentucky’s eminent domain rules. The Kentucky Legislature recently passed House Bill 542, which places further restrictions on how and when eminent domain can be used. Woodall said the law focuses on property taking involving conservation easements and agricultural districts.Under those circumstances, the government entity would have to prove that taking the property is the only route available.You use AI every day.
